article.title: Feds Suspect Ransom Negotiator Ran ShinyHunters Extortion Site
article.summary: U.S. federal investigators pursuing the ShinyHunters hacking group that recently stole highly sensitive data from the FBI have identified executives at two different ransomware negotiation firms who maintained unusually close relations with the extortion group, KrebsOnSecurity has learned. Sources close to the investigation say one of the executives in the United States even helped ShinyHunters operate a website that pressured victims into paying a ransom.
article.raw_text: Feds Suspect Ransom Negotiator Ran ShinyHunters Extortion Site U.S. federal investigators pursuing the ShinyHunters hacking group that recently stole highly sensitive data from the FBI have identified executives at two different ransomware negotiation firms who maintained unusually close relations with the extortion group, KrebsOnSecurity has learned. Sources close to the investigation say one of the executives in the United States even helped ShinyHunters operate a website that pressured victims into paying a ransom. U.S. federal investigators pursuing the ShinyHunters hacking group that recently stole highly sensitive data from the FBI have identified executives at two different ransomware negotiation firms who maintained unusually close relations with the extortion group, KrebsOnSecurity has learned. Sources close to the investigation say one of the executives in the United States even helped ShinyHunters operate a website that pressured victims into paying a ransom. Hackers aligned with ShinyHunters have claimed credit for dozens of major data breaches since 2019, when the group was primarily operated by cybercriminals living in France. As those original members were arrested or jailed one by one, control over the ShinyHunters brand eventually passed to “ Rey ,” identified last year as a teenage hacker from Amman, Jordan. According to the FBI, ShinyHunters has extorted more than $70 million from victims so far this year. In late September, ShinyHunters hacked the FBI recruitment website fbijobs.gov and taunted the agency by threatening to publish the stolen files, which reportedly included medical and psychological records, Social Security numbers and home addresses, and information about each employee’s unit and specialization. The FBI jobs site hack has prompted the agency to move with uncommon speed to arrest, detain and question people who had any communications with Rey or other ShinyHunters suspects. Reuters reported on October 3 that Rey had been detained by Jordanian authorities and was cooperating with the FBI. Rey was able to assume control over the hacking group because one of its alleged senior members had just been nabbed. On the evening of September 15, 2026, authorities in the Netherlands arrested convicted hacker and ShinyHunters suspect Pepijn van der Stap . Dutch police reportedly used flash-bang grenades in an effort to stun and apprehend Van der Stap as he was logged in to various online accounts. According to a source close to the investigation, the authorities arrested Van der Stap while he was using his Signal instant messaging account, which allowed them to read recent communications with frequent contacts — including ransomware negotiators based in Canada and the United States. Multiple sources with knowledge of the matter told KrebsOnSecurity that Van der Stap’s messages were the key to unraveling a murder-for-hire plot that emerged immediately following his arrest. The Dutch news outlet RTL reported last month the two murders were allegedly to be committed abroad, and that there are indications Van der Stap gave the order for the attacks (there is no indication those orders were ever carried out). On October 9, KrebsOnSecurity broke the news that the FBI arrested a 54-year-old Canadian cybersecurity executive named Edward Dubrovsky in connection with the ShinyHunters investigation. Dubrovsky, who recently published a book on handling cyber extortion that recommended always engaging with the hackers, was charged with threatening to disclose stolen or hacked data and interfering with interstate commerce through extortion, according to court records . Politico reports prosecutors have asked that Dubrovsky remain in custody pending trial, and that records related to his case remain under seal. A source close to the investigation told KrebsOnSecurity that Van der Stap’s Signal messages showed he had frequent conversations with Mr. Dubrovsky and with at least one executive at a large U.S.-based consulting firm, and that these executives often knew the details about new ShinyHunters victims before the victims themselves had even learned of the breach. That source shared another potentially explosive finding by federal investigators: the Dutch hacker’s chats showed Mr. Dubrovsky knew ShinyHunters had stolen highly sensitive data from FBI servers, and that he never informed the bureau of the data breach prior to ShinyHunters threatening on Twitter/X to publish the agency’s deeply personal personnel files. SHINYWIRE KrebsOnSecurity has learned from two sources close to the ShinyHunters probe that FBI investigators believe at least one executive at a U.S.-based consulting firm played an active role in operating the now-defunct ShinyHunters victim extortion website “ shinywire[.]com .” KrebsOnSecurity is not naming the U.S. company or the suspected executive(s) for now because they have not yet been charged with a crime, but it is a prestigious firm with more than 1,000 associates. A section of the homepage for the now-defunct Shinywire website. The Shinywire website was active from approximately May 3, 2026 until October 16 and had entries for nearly 100 organizations hacked by ShinyHunters. Each entry urged victims to engage with the cybercrime group and discuss terms for payment. The pages also included samples of stolen files and promised those files would be published online if the victim ignored their demands. The following screenshot shows a cached portion of the Shinywire extortion page for Intuitive Surgical , an American medical technology company that was breached in March 2026 after an employee fell for a targeted phishing email. The Shinywire website, as indexed by urlscan.io. This listing is an extortion demand targeting Intuitive Surgical, an American medical technology company breached in March 2026 by a targeted phishing email attack that compromised an employee’s credentials. Victim organizations that refused to engage or negotiate after seven days would find all of their stolen data published on the ShinyHunters victim shaming blog (a website that is only reachable via the anonymity network Tor ). In a story published October 15, The Globe and Mail wrote that a few months before Edward Dubrovsky was arrested by the FBI, the Canadian cybersecurity executive alleged in court documents he had become collateral damage in a campaign by a former business partner to “destroy” another industry executive. The story noted that Dubrovsky filed the lawsuit in Ontario this year against Daniel Tobok , the former chief executive of Cypfer , a cybersecurity firm founded in Toronto with offices in the U.S., Britain, the Netherlands, the United Arab Emirates, and Mexico. The two first became business partners in 2017 and later developed Cypfer together, where Mr. Dubrovsky was a managing partner and chief operating officer. But by 2024, the two had a falling out, with Dubrovsky accusing Tobok of gradually excluding him from business matters and making “increasingly capricious business decisions.” Mr. Tobok reportedly denied the allegations and filed a counterclaim, accusing Mr. Dubrovsky of accessing confidential information and unfairly competing with Cypfer through work at another firm called CyberSteward Inc . He also said Mr. Dubrovsky has misrepresented himself as a Cypfer founder, and is not a shareholder. GHOSTBYTE According to interviews with several former colleagues of Mr. Tobok, as far back as eight years ago he was known to ransomware purveyors by a particular nickname: Ghostbyte . In 2018, a Canadian company was hacked by Dharma , a prolific Russian-language ransomware affiliate program that first surfaced in 2016. The victim company told the Dharma ransomware representative they were leaning toward paying because some of the files were unrecoverable after being locked, but that they needed a better guarantee that Dharma would keep their word if paid. A redacted copy of the Dharma rep’s reply is pictured below, and it shows the ransomware group urged the victim to contact a person at a Canadian IT firm that helps companies seeking such guarantees. The Dharma rep recommended the victim contact the email address ghostbyte@tutanota.com . “If you want guarantees, you can write to the IT company,” the Dharma reply advised. “Take the phone and negotiate with them. This IT company often solves such problems in Canada. You can contact them and sign a contract for services. You’ll still have to pay.” An email reply from the Dharma ransomware group to a victim, recommending they contact an email address that is connected to Mr. Tobok. It’s unclear if Mr. Tobok ever used that Ghostbyte address offered by the Dharma representative, and he has not responded to multiple requests for comment. However, the breach tracking service Constella Intelligence finds an email address Mr. Tobok has frequently used — dtobok@me.com — is associated with two online accounts where the chosen username was “ghostbyte,” including a Snapchat account. Incidentally, Constella also finds the Dharma rep’s email address luckygoodlucky@tuta.io is associated with a cryptocurrency address that processed 38 transactions totaling 43 bitcoin, ~$3.5 million at today’s value (the most recent transaction for this wallet is dated February 2019). In a statement shared on October 14, Cypfer said the company’s business does not include making or facilitating ransomware payments, and that Cypfer learned of Dubrovsky’s arrest when the news first broke in the media. “We had no prior knowledge of Mr. Dubrovsky’s arrest,” a spokesperson told KrebsOnSecurity via email. “ CYPFER has not received any outreach from law enforcement and, to our knowledge, is not the target of any law enforcement investigation.” The statement said CyberSteward and Cypfer are separate companies with no officers, directors or employees in common, and that Cypfer was recently acquired by the Apros Group , a holding company led by Jason Hogg , a former FBI special agent and former CEO of Aon Cyber Solutions Group . In 2020, Aon aquired Cytelligence , a security consulting firm where Mr. Tobok was founder and CEO and Mr. Dubrovsky was a managing partner. CONFLICTING INTERESTS It is not illegal in the United States to pay hackers for an encryption key to unlock servers infected with ransomware, or in exchange for a promise to delete any stolen files and refrain from publishing them online. While victim organizations can land in legal hot water if they pay a ransom to a group that is sanctioned by the U.S. Treasury Department, ShinyHunters is not among the ransomware groups currently sanctioned by the United States or by any other government. Experts say ransomware victims are typically directed by their insurance provider to work with a specific incident response firm. But not all cyber forensics and breach response companies will agree to facilitate payments to ransomware groups on behalf of their clients. As a result, once victim firms make a decision to pay, the firms that eschew rewarding extortionists are invariably replaced by companies that have no such qualms. In December 2024, ShinyHunters began extorting the education technology company PowerSchool , stealing private information on 62 million students and 9.5 million teachers in the U.S. and Canada. PowerSchool reportedly paid a $2.85 million ransom demand, and a “frequently asked questions” statement (PDF) about the breach says PowerSchool was assisted in that effort by CyberSteward (ShinyHunters affiliate Matthew Lane , 20, of Sterling, Mass., was sentenced in November 2025 to four years in prison for his admitted role in the PowerSchool hack). But that ransom payment did not stop future extortion attempts using the same stolen data. By May 2025, individual school districts were reportedly receiving separate ransom demands using samples of the same stolen files. While nobody has alleged ShinyHunters was behind the second wave of extortion against PowerSchool users, the incident drives home the reality that there is no technical way to verify the threat actors have deleted the stolen data as promised, or prevent others from abusing the same records. A number of leading cyber incident response firms, including Coveware and Unit 221B , have consistently warned victims against paying ShinyHunters , noting that “destroyed” victim data is often kept, resold or used to extort the company’s clients directly later on. The FBI echoed those sentiments in an alert on May 15, 2026 advising victims against paying the ShinyHunters group. Meanwhile, ShinyHunters members have been harassing and threatening employees at Coveware and Unit 221B for offering this advice. The following screenshots show just how annoyed the ShinyHunters leaders were with Coveware’s relentless advice against paying the group. The first image is from a conversation on May 6, 2026 that took place between the group’s main account on Telegram and a co-conspirator. In that chat, snippets of which were shared with KrebsOnSecurity by a trusted source, ShinyHunters complained that Coveware was harming the group’s payment rates. The operator of the ShinyHunters account on Telegram speaking privately with a co-conspirator and complaining that Coveware was harming their business. “Go on my website, majority of those companies would’ve paid if it weren’t for Coveware giving them misinformation,” the ShinyHunters account wrote. “Someone (100% Coveware) is going out of their way to make sure i am not paid.” In another conversation on April 11, 2026, the ShinyHunters Telegram account privately said they were trying to “eliminate the problem,” which they said was Coveware. “I’m sure the company will pay but in this specific case I am aware of Coveware and their involvement, and I’ve probably been not getting a lot of other negotiations mostly likely because Coveware keeps getting involved,” the ShinyHunters account bemoaned. The operator of the ShinyHunters account on Telegram telling a co-conspirator they were “trying to eliminate the problem,” which they identified as Coveware advising victims not to pay the cybercrime group. Coveware CEO Bill Siegel said he was unable to comment on anything related to past clients or ShinyHunters, beyond stating that the FBI has notified the affected victims of Van der Stap’s alleged murder-for-hire scheme, and that no Coveware employees were notified. Mark Camillo is chief executive at CyberAcuView , an industry group founded in 2021 by a consortium of major cyber insurance carriers. Camillo said some firms charge a flat retainer fee, while those that specialize in helping companies negotiate a ransom payment tend to charge a percentage of the total ransom amount paid. That latter dynamic, he said, is an inherent conflict of interest, as the negotiator has every incentive to make things more favorable to the attackers because they are financially incentivized to negotiate and pay out, and to not negotiate down on the price. “It has come to the industry’s attention that many of the ransomware payers charge a percentage of the final payment which may or may not be disclosed,” Camillo said. “This makes no sense if they are also the negotiator. There needs to be more transparency in the process as no one in the ecosystem should be profiting purely on the size of the ransomware transaction or payment itself.” Camillo said the firms doing this work would argue the fees are needed because there may be unexpectedly higher costs to secure larger quantities of cryptocurrency or more risk carrying the float, and because cryptocurrency exchanges may charge higher fees for high risk transactions. “There definitely needs to be more visibility around the transaction and clarity on the increasing value of the crypto and the exchange’s percent in the transaction to get to the bottom of this and remove any misaligned incentives,” he said. In recent months, the U.S. Department of Justice has prosecuted a number of ransomware negotiators alleged to have conspired with cybercriminals to defraud their clients. On October 7, the DOJ charged MonsterCloud CEO Zohar Pinhasi , 50, with wire fraud and conspiracy for allegedly charging customers to remediate ransomware attacks without paying the hackers. According to charging documents, Pinhasi secretly went behind his customers’ backs and paid hackers anyway, paying ransomware groups $8 million while charging customers $19 million. In July, Angelo Martino , a 41-year-old ransomware negotiator from Land O’Lakes, Florida, was sentenced to 70 months in prison for conspiring with the Blackcat/ALPHV ransomware group to extort multiple victims. According to the DOJ, Martino was paid by BlackCat attackers to provide confidential information about the negotiating position and strategy of his employer’s clients and enable the ransomware actors to maximize the ransoms paid by the victims.

hypotheses.title: Initial access via the disclosed vulnerability affecting Microsoft Exchange
hypotheses.statement: A threat actor has attempted to obtain initial access to our environment by exploiting the disclosed vulnerability in Microsoft Exchange within the last 30 days.
hypotheses.rationale: Archetype 'initial_access_cve' selected based on malware families: BlackCat / ALPHV; vectors: phishing, exploit; impact: ransomware, data-breach, fraud; products: Microsoft Exchange.

objectives.title: Inventory exposure to Microsoft Exchange
objectives.falsification_criterion: If zero internet-facing assets run a vulnerable build of Microsoft Exchange, the external-exploitation hypothesis is disproven for the referenced CVE.
objectives.suggested_query: asset_inventory | where product == 'Microsoft Exchange' and exposure == 'internet' and version in (vulnerable_versions)

objectives.title: Hunt for exploit attempts at the edge
objectives.falsification_criterion: If WAF / firewall / IDS show no exploit-signature hits for the referenced CVE in the last 30 days, in-the-wild exploitation against us is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: edge_logs | where signature contains 'CVE' or uri matches /exploit-pattern-for-the referenced CVE/ | summarize count() by src_ip, dst_host

objectives.title: Patch-status correlation
objectives.falsification_criterion: If MDM / patch-management shows 100% deployment of the the referenced CVE fix across exposed hosts, the hypothesis is disproven by remediation.
objectives.suggested_query: patch_state | where kb in (fixes_for('the referenced CVE')) | summarize coverage = avg(installed) by host_role

objectives.title: Post-exploit web-shell sweep
objectives.falsification_criterion: If a sweep of webroots and IIS/Apache process trees finds no anomalous children (cmd, powershell, /bin/sh) on Microsoft Exchange hosts, post-exploit foothold is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: process | where parent in ('w3wp.exe','httpd','nginx','java') and child in ('cmd.exe','powershell.exe','/bin/sh','/bin/bash')

objectives.title: Honeypot / canary check
objectives.falsification_criterion: If exposed canary instances of the same product show no probing or exploitation telemetry, opportunistic mass-exploitation against the org is unlikely.
objectives.suggested_query: canary_events | where product == '<product>' | where event_type in ('probe','exploit') | summarize by src_ip

hypotheses.title: Endpoint execution of BlackCat / ALPHV
hypotheses.statement: One or more endpoints in the estate have executed or attempted to execute BlackCat / ALPHV payloads since the reporting date.
hypotheses.rationale: Archetype 'malware_execution' selected based on malware families: BlackCat / ALPHV; vectors: phishing, exploit; impact: ransomware, data-breach, fraud; products: Microsoft Exchange.

objectives.title: EDR hash sweep for BlackCat / ALPHV
objectives.falsification_criterion: If a search of EDR file/process telemetry for known BlackCat / ALPHV SHA256s returns zero hits in the last 90 days, payload presence is disproven.
objectives.suggested_query: process_events | where sha256 in (ti_lookup('BlackCat / ALPHV', 'sha256')) | summarize count() by host

objectives.title: Behavioural pattern hunt for BlackCat / ALPHV
objectives.falsification_criterion: If parent/child anomalies typical of the family (e.g. Office spawning script hosts, rundll32 chains) are absent across the estate, execution chain is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: process | where parent in ('winword.exe','excel.exe','outlook.exe') and child in ('rundll32.exe','wscript.exe','mshta.exe','powershell.exe')

objectives.title: Persistence-key inspection
objectives.falsification_criterion: If autoruns, scheduled tasks, services, and WMI subscriptions show no BlackCat / ALPHV-aligned artifacts, post-execution persistence is disproven.
objectives.suggested_query: registry_set | where key matches /Run|RunOnce|Image File Execution Options/ and value matches /unusual-path/

objectives.title: AV / quarantine retrospective
objectives.falsification_criterion: If retrospective AV / quarantine logs show no detections for related signatures over the last 30 days, the family is unlikely to have landed in-environment.
objectives.suggested_query: av_events | where signature contains 'BlackCat / ALPHV' | summarize by host, action

objectives.title: Memory-resident loader check
objectives.falsification_criterion: If a memory scan (YARA via EDR / Volatility) finds none of the published loader patterns on a sampled set of high-risk hosts, in-memory residency is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: memory_scan | yara_rule == 'rule_blackcat_/_alphv' | summarize by host

hypotheses.title: Outbound C2 beaconing to reported infrastructure
hypotheses.statement: Hosts in the estate are beaconing to the command-and-control infrastructure reported in this article (domains, IPs, TLS fingerprints, or RMM tooling).
hypotheses.rationale: Archetype 'c2_beacon' selected based on malware families: BlackCat / ALPHV; vectors: phishing, exploit; impact: ransomware, data-breach, fraud; products: Microsoft Exchange.

objectives.title: DNS resolution sweep for published C2 domains
objectives.falsification_criterion: If recursive DNS logs show zero resolutions for the IOC domains in the last 90 days, active beaconing is disproven.
objectives.suggested_query: dns | where query in ('fbijobs.gov','shinywire.com','urlscan.io') | summarize count() by client_ip

objectives.title: Egress connections to published C2 IPs
objectives.falsification_criterion: If proxy / firewall egress logs show no connections to the IOC IPs or matching ASNs, network-level C2 is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: egress | where dst_ip in ('the published C2 IPs') | summarize bytes_out = sum(bytes_sent) by src_ip

objectives.title: Beacon periodicity / jitter analysis
objectives.falsification_criterion: If beacon-style periodic outbound connections (low jitter, small payloads) to uncategorised destinations are absent, covert C2 is unlikely.
objectives.suggested_query: conn | summarize stddev_interval = stdev(diff(ts)), count() by src_ip, dst_host | where count() > 50 and stddev_interval < 5s

objectives.title: TLS / JA3 fingerprint pivot
objectives.falsification_criterion: If JA3/JA3S fingerprints associated with the reported family are absent in TLS telemetry, encrypted C2 attribution is weakened.
objectives.suggested_query: tls | where ja3 in (ti_lookup('family','ja3')) | summarize by src_ip, sni

objectives.title: Remote-monitoring tooling abuse check
objectives.falsification_criterion: If unmanaged AnyDesk / TeamViewer / ScreenConnect / Atera installs are absent, RMM-based C2 is disproven.
objectives.suggested_query: process | where name in ('anydesk.exe','teamviewer.exe','screenconnect.exe','atera*.exe') and signer != 'corp_managed'

hypotheses.title: Post-foothold lateral movement consistent with the reported actor
hypotheses.statement: An attacker who matched the TTPs of the reported actor has moved laterally inside the estate using RDP/SMB/WinRM, admin tooling, or Kerberos abuse.
hypotheses.rationale: Archetype 'lateral_movement' selected based on malware families: BlackCat / ALPHV; vectors: phishing, exploit; impact: ransomware, data-breach, fraud; products: Microsoft Exchange.

objectives.title: Anomalous remote logons (Type 3 / Type 10)
objectives.falsification_criterion: If 4624 logon-type 3/10 events show no bursts from a single source to many destinations, lateral movement via RDP/SMB is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: security | where event_id in (4624) and logon_type in (3,10) | summarize dests = dcount(dst_host) by src_user, src_host | where dests > 10

objectives.title: Admin-tool usage outside baseline
objectives.falsification_criterion: If PsExec / WMIC / PowerShell remoting / Impacket-style usage is absent outside known admin jump-hosts, the lateral-tool hypothesis is disproven.
objectives.suggested_query: process | where name in ('psexec.exe','psexesvc.exe','wmic.exe','wsmprovhost.exe') and host !in (admin_jumphosts)

objectives.title: Kerberos abuse telemetry
objectives.falsification_criterion: If 4769 ticket requests show no anomalous RC4 / odd-SPN patterns and no AS-REP roasting indicators, credential-based lateral movement is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: security | where event_id == 4769 and ticket_encryption == 'RC4-HMAC' | summarize by target_spn, account_name

objectives.title: Lateral file-copy staging
objectives.falsification_criterion: If SMB writes of archives / executables across multiple hosts from one user/host are absent, lateral staging is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: file | where action == 'write' and ext in ('.7z','.rar','.zip','.exe') and dest matches /\\\\.*\\(C\$|admin\$)/

article.title: Siemens RUGGEDCOM CROSSBOW
article.summary: View CSAF Summary RUGGEDCOM CROSSBOW contains multiple vulnerabilities that could allow an attacker to execute arbitrary SQL commands on the underlying database, retrieve sensitive administrative credentials, escalate privileges, and perform unauthorized operations such as modifying system configurations or causing a denial of service. Siemens has released a new version for RUGGEDCOM CROSSBOW and recommends to update to the latest version. The following versions of Siemens RUGGEDCOM CROSSBOW are affected: RUGGEDCOM CROSSBOW vers:intdot/ CVSS Vendor Equipment v3 8.8 Siemens RUGGEDCOM CROSSBOW 4 Vulnerabilities Improper Neutralization of Special Elements used in an SQL Command ('SQL Injection'), Authorization Bypass Through User-Controlled Key, Insertion of Sensitive Information Into Sent Data, Client-Side Enforcement of Server-Side Security Background Critical Infrastructure Sectors: Critical Manufacturing, Transportation Systems, Energy, Healthcare and Public Health, Financial Services, Government Services and Facilities Countries/Areas Deployed: Worldwide Company Headquarters Location: Germany Vulnerabilities Expand All + CVE-2026-89196 Affected devices do not properly validate or sanitize input in facility names processed during the Bulk Import/Export workflow. This could allow an authenticated attacker with specific privileges to execute arbitrary SQL commands on the underlying database. Read More 1 Affected Product RUGGEDCOM CROSSBOW Product Status: known_affected Remedia

Minimize network exposure for all control system devices and/or systems, ensuring they are not accessible from the internet . Locate control system networks and remote devices behind firewalls and isolating them from business networks. When remote access is required, use more secure methods, such as Virtual Private Networks (VPNs), recognizing VPNs may have vulnerabilities and should be updated to the most current version available. Also recognize VPN is only as secure as the connected devices. CISA reminds organizations to perform proper impact analysis and risk assessment prior to deploying defensive measures. CISA also provides a section for control systems security recommended practices on the ICS webpage on cisa.gov/ics . Several CISA products detailing cyber defense best practices are available for reading and download, including Improving Industrial Control Systems Cybersecurity with Defense-in-Depth Strategies . CISA encourages organizations to implement recommended cybersecurity strategies for proactive defense of ICS assets . Additional mitigation guidance and recommended practices are publicly available on the ICS webpage at cisa.gov/ics in the technical information paper, ICS-TIP-12-146-01B--Targeted Cyber Intrusion Detection and Mitigation Strategies . Organizations observing suspected malicious activity should follow established internal procedures and report findings to CISA for tracking and correlation against other incidents. hypotheses.title: Initial access via CVE-2026-89196 affecting the affected product/service
hypotheses.statement: A threat actor has attempted to obtain initial access to our environment by exploiting CVE-2026-89196 in the affected product/service within the last 30 days.
hypotheses.rationale: Archetype 'initial_access_cve' selected based on CVEs cited: CVE-2026-89196, CVE-2026-89197, CVE-2026-89198; vectors: exploit, vpn-edge; impact: ddos.

objectives.title: Inventory exposure to the affected product
objectives.falsification_criterion: If zero internet-facing assets run a vulnerable build of the affected product, the external-exploitation hypothesis is disproven for CVE-2026-89196.
objectives.suggested_query: asset_inventory | where product == 'the affected product' and exposure == 'internet' and version in (vulnerable_versions)

objectives.title: Hunt for exploit attempts at the edge
objectives.falsification_criterion: If WAF / firewall / IDS show no exploit-signature hits for CVE-2026-89196 in the last 30 days, in-the-wild exploitation against us is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: edge_logs | where signature contains 'CVE' or uri matches /exploit-pattern-for-CVE-2026-89196/ | summarize count() by src_ip, dst_host

objectives.title: Patch-status correlation
objectives.falsification_criterion: If MDM / patch-management shows 100% deployment of the CVE-2026-89196 fix across exposed hosts, the hypothesis is disproven by remediation.
objectives.suggested_query: patch_state | where kb in (fixes_for('CVE-2026-89196')) | summarize coverage = avg(installed) by host_role

objectives.title: Post-exploit web-shell sweep
objectives.falsification_criterion: If a sweep of webroots and IIS/Apache process trees finds no anomalous children (cmd, powershell, /bin/sh) on the affected product hosts, post-exploit foothold is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: process | where parent in ('w3wp.exe','httpd','nginx','java') and child in ('cmd.exe','powershell.exe','/bin/sh','/bin/bash')

objectives.title: Honeypot / canary check
objectives.falsification_criterion: If exposed canary instances of the same product show no probing or exploitation telemetry, opportunistic mass-exploitation against the org is unlikely.
objectives.suggested_query: canary_events | where product == '<product>' | where event_type in ('probe','exploit') | summarize by src_ip

hypotheses.title: Outbound C2 beaconing to reported infrastructure
hypotheses.statement: Hosts in the estate are beaconing to the command-and-control infrastructure reported in this article (domains, IPs, TLS fingerprints, or RMM tooling).
hypotheses.rationale: Archetype 'c2_beacon' selected based on CVEs cited: CVE-2026-89196, CVE-2026-89197, CVE-2026-89198; vectors: exploit, vpn-edge; impact: ddos.

objectives.title: DNS resolution sweep for published C2 domains
objectives.falsification_criterion: If recursive DNS logs show zero resolutions for the IOC domains in the last 90 days, active beaconing is disproven.
objectives.suggested_query: dns | where query in ('www.siemens.com') | summarize count() by client_ip

objectives.title: Egress connections to published C2 IPs
objectives.falsification_criterion: If proxy / firewall egress logs show no connections to the IOC IPs or matching ASNs, network-level C2 is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: egress | where dst_ip in ('the published C2 IPs') | summarize bytes_out = sum(bytes_sent) by src_ip

objectives.title: Beacon periodicity / jitter analysis
objectives.falsification_criterion: If beacon-style periodic outbound connections (low jitter, small payloads) to uncategorised destinations are absent, covert C2 is unlikely.
objectives.suggested_query: conn | summarize stddev_interval = stdev(diff(ts)), count() by src_ip, dst_host | where count() > 50 and stddev_interval < 5s

objectives.title: TLS / JA3 fingerprint pivot
objectives.falsification_criterion: If JA3/JA3S fingerprints associated with the reported family are absent in TLS telemetry, encrypted C2 attribution is weakened.
objectives.suggested_query: tls | where ja3 in (ti_lookup('family','ja3')) | summarize by src_ip, sni

objectives.title: Remote-monitoring tooling abuse check
objectives.falsification_criterion: If unmanaged AnyDesk / TeamViewer / ScreenConnect / Atera installs are absent, RMM-based C2 is disproven.
objectives.suggested_query: process | where name in ('anydesk.exe','teamviewer.exe','screenconnect.exe','atera*.exe') and signer != 'corp_managed'

hypotheses.title: Identity compromise of privileged users
hypotheses.statement: Privileged identities have been compromised through phishing, MFA fatigue, help-desk social engineering, or OAuth illicit-consent grants.
hypotheses.rationale: Archetype 'identity_compromise' selected based on CVEs cited: CVE-2026-89196, CVE-2026-89197, CVE-2026-89198; vectors: exploit, vpn-edge; impact: ddos.

objectives.title: Impossible-travel / atypical sign-ins
objectives.falsification_criterion: If Entra ID / Okta risky-sign-in detections show no impossible-travel hits on privileged identities, account compromise is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: signin | where risk_level in ('high','medium') and user in (privileged_users) | summarize by country, ip

objectives.title: MFA-fatigue / push-bombing
objectives.falsification_criterion: If MFA telemetry shows no bursts of denied pushes followed by a successful one for the same user, MFA-fatigue compromise is disproven.
objectives.suggested_query: mfa | summarize denies = countif(result=='deny'), accepts = countif(result=='accept') by user, bin(ts,1h) | where denies > 5 and accepts > 0

objectives.title: Help-desk social-engineering pivot
objectives.falsification_criterion: If ticketing / call-recording shows no recent password-reset or MFA-reset requests for privileged users without proper verification, help-desk vector is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: tickets | where action in ('password_reset','mfa_reset') and target in (privileged_users) | join (verifications) on ticket_id

objectives.title: OAuth illicit-consent grants
objectives.falsification_criterion: If Entra/Workspace audit logs show no recently consented third-party apps with high-impact scopes, OAuth abuse is disproven.
objectives.suggested_query: audit | where action == 'Consent to application' and scopes contains 'Mail.Read' or 'files.read.all'

article.title: AI-driven, large-scale nation-state campaign using ARTEX enables supply chain compromise
article.summary: Storm-0940 used ARTEX agentic AI to accelerate a ConnectWise supply chain compromise, enabling application credential abuse across Microsoft 365 environments. The post AI-driven, large-scale nation-state campaign using ARTEX enables supply chain compromise appeared first on Microsoft Security Blog .
article.raw_text: AI-driven, large-scale nation-state campaign using ARTEX enables supply chain compromise Storm-0940 used ARTEX agentic AI to accelerate a ConnectWise supply chain compromise, enabling application credential abuse across Microsoft 365 environments. The post AI-driven, large-scale nation-state campaign using ARTEX enables supply chain compromise appeared first on Microsoft Security Blog . In this article What’s happening What is ARTEX? Mitigation and protection guidance References Learn more As early as September 2026, Storm-0940, a China-state aligned actor, used the agentic AI penetration testing framework ARTEX to automate attacks targeting hundreds of organizations globally across a broad range of industries. Several of these Storm-0940 ARTEX-driven attacks have resulted in the actor obtaining privileged access to an organization’s cloud infrastructure – including multiple instances where the time from initial targeting to privileged access was less than 3 hours. Microsoft assesses that Storm-0940 was responsible for the recently disclosed ConnectWise supply chain compromise of a multi-tenant application. This activity demonstrates how threat actors are integrating agentic AI into existing offensive security workflows and allows them to scale their operations exponentially. Agents are not constrained by factors affecting humans – they can work around the clock, on weekends, and on holidays and attempt multiple breach paths simultaneously enabling significantly reduced time from selecting a target to achieving objectives, increasing the speed and impact of complex attacks like supply chain compromises. Storm-0940’s use of ARTEX accelerated the speed of compromised application abuse to authenticate to Microsoft 365 customer environments through applications that had already been granted access. This allowed the threat actor to operate without requiring an interactive user sign-in. In multiple affected environments, Microsoft observed AI-accelerated follow-on activity through Microsoft Graph, including reconnaissance, application credential changes, and attempts to modify privileges that could enable expanded or persistent access. The activity conducted by the threat actor through the usage of ARTEX framework did not result from a compromise of or a vulnerability in Microsoft corporate systems, products, or services. Although Microsoft identified Storm-0940-initiated authentication and follow-on activity in multiple customer environments, the presence of an affected application or successful threat actor authentication does not necessarily indicate that customer data was accessed or exfiltrated. Microsoft Defender XDR provides detections and hunting queries for suspicious Microsoft Graph activity and activity associated with known threat infrastructure. Customers should review service principal sign-ins, investigate unexpected application credential or privilege changes, and follow ConnectWise’s published containment guidance while preserving relevant evidence for investigation. For a full list of detections please see the detections section. What’s happening Storm-0940 is a China-state aligned actor (with no known industry aliases) that has been active since 2021 and targets organizations across multiple industries for data theft. The actor has historically gained initial access using password spraying and exploitation of internet-facing applications, before using compromised accounts to move through targeted environments. In cloud environments, the actor has also established persistence by adding credentials to existing OAuth applications, allowing continued access to Microsoft 365 resources. The actor has used these applications to access and exfiltrate email and other data through Microsoft Graph. As early as September 2026, Storm-0940 used the agentic AI penetration testing framework ARTEX to automate attacks targeting hundreds of organizations globally across a broad range of industries. These include aerospace and defense, automotive, chemicals, energy, financial services, government, legal, manufacturing, media, military, semiconductor, software, technology, and think tanks and non-profits. During the ConnectWise supply chain compromise, Storm-0940 used ARTEX to accelerate scanning and reconnaissance, password spraying, and OAuth application abuse at downstream victims. Several of these Storm-0940 ARTEX-driven attacks have resulted in the actor obtaining privileged access to an organization’s cloud infrastructure – including multiple instances where the time from initial targeting to privileged access was less than 3 hours. When automated with AI, these activities generate a large volume of traffic and log data that may generate alerts. However, the speed of the activity allows very little time for Defenders to respond to those alerts and remediate the actor’s access in a coordinated fashion. Storm-0940’s activity illustrates how a threat actor with a broad target set can use an agentic AI tool and privileged authentication material to quickly attempt to compromise many organizations. While the majority of the targeting wasn’t successful, Storm-0940 achieved privileged cloud persistence at many organizations in a brief time. What is ARTEX? ARTEX is an open-source penetration testing framework that can use any AI model to automate a variety of offensive security workflows. The ARTEX framework is a multi-agent LLM system written in GO with a Next.js frontend. While the UI and generated output default to English, the framework can be switched to Korean, Mandarin, Spanish, or Japanese. ARTEX is a system of LLM-driven agents that run an autonomous penetration test from reconnaissance through data exfiltration with little needed human interaction. The agents then accumulate the discovered assets and vulnerabilities into a graph during the penetration test. In October 2026, public reporting noted that the ARTEX framework was being used by threat actors, such as the personal data breaches targeting Korean financial institutions. Microsoft Threat Intelligence has identified threat actors across multiple geographic regions leveraging the ARTEX framework. On October 16, 2026, ConnectWise publicly reported unauthorized access to its customers’ tenants using multiple OAuth application identities. Following the unauthorized access, Storm-0940 used ARTEX to reach more than 2,250 tenants at 2,900 sign-in attempts per minute, a pace that leaves defenders with little time to detect and respond. While OAuth application abuse is a typical part of Storm-0940’s toolset, in this case the actor used ARTEX to accelerate the activity to machine speed. Figure 1. Scale and speed of a subset of Storm-0940’s automated ARTEX campaign on downstream tenants, including tenant reach and rapid sign-ins. Password Spraying Between October 10 and 14, 2026, Storm-0940 infrastructure at 144.172.64[.]99 conducted an automated cross-tenant password-spray campaign targeting 327 accounts across eight organizations to gain access to Microsoft 365 and Exchange Online. During this large campaign, Microsoft telemetry captured 151,000+ failed logon events, with activity peaking on October 11 at 2,900 failures per minute and concentrating more than 111,000 failures into a single day. The campaign blended broad, low-rate account spraying with sustained, high-volume authentication attempts against selected identities; 48 accounts received more than 1,000 failures, and lockout responses represented nearly 98% of all activity. Despite the scale, no successful authentication, token issuance, Graph call, or directory change was observed. Downstream customer access On October 15, immediately after this notable activity, public reports of the compromise of the popular cloud backup application ConnectWise started to surface with direct references to indicators of compromise matching the same network range observed for the earlier password-spray campaign (144.172.64.x). An advisory from the affected cloud backup vendor posted on October 16 shared later additional indicators with one IP address matching exactly the 144.172.64[.]99 infrastructure responsible for the earlier password-spray campaign. Additionally, after acquiring control of the identities of multiple ConnectWise cloud applications, the AI agents operating on behalf of the threat actor continued to use the same IP range to authenticate to customer environments using the illicit access acquired through these stolen app credentials, effectively taking advantage of the already established trust by these apps within a tenant. In some of these environments, the AI agents (on behalf of the threat actor) progressed beyond authentication to Microsoft Graph and directory operations, including reconnaissance, application credential modifications to establish persistence, and changes involving identities, groups, and privileged roles. Microsoft identified multiple customer environments with evidence of follow-on activity, highlighting how a compromised third-party application with high privileges could provide access beyond its originally intended purpose. The application credential modification made by Storm-0940’s associated agents in the targeted victims’ environments can lead to persistence through other identities, credentials, and cloud services. These changes can remain active as a backdoor even after the original compromised application is mediated. Organizations should examine service principal sign-ins alongside subsequent Microsoft Graph activity, directory changes, and resource access, correlating suspicious events with authorized administrative activity. The presence of an affected application, or even successful authentication, does not necessarily indicate unauthorized data access or data exfiltration. Mitigation and protection guidance Microsoft recommends the following mitigations to reduce the impact of this threat. Check the recommendations card for the deployment status of monitored mitigations. Immediate actions Keep affected ConnectWise application connections disabled until ConnectWise provides formal restoration instructions. Do not delete enterprise applications as the first response. Preserve configuration and evidence before making irreversible changes. Inventory all four application IDs listed in this profile and record the local service-principal Object ID in each tenant. Review every Microsoft 365 tenant where the affected applications are currently or were previously installed or authorized, even if the integration is no longer in use. Search by application ID rather than display name. Preserve available Microsoft Entra sign-in and audit records , Microsoft Purview Audit records, SIEM data, and previously configured Microsoft Graph telemetry. Do not delay urgent containment while waiting for exports. Review activity starting from at least October 15, 2026. Where records are available, extend service-principal sign-in review to October 1 and investigate earlier related activity, including failed authentications and volume anomalies. Review successful and failed service-principal sign-ins separately. Investigate unfamiliar sources and activity outside expected vendor infrastructure; do not limit review to the published IPs. Review Microsoft Entra audit records for application or service-principal credential additions; new applications, service principals, or owners; app-role assignments and consent grants; privileged role assignments; and changes to users, groups, authentication methods, or Conditional Access. On confirmed suspicious activity, revoke unnecessary permissions and rotate credentials. Review Microsoft 365 audit records to look for reconnaissance activities like listing directories, permissions, and approvals coming from unusual IPs. Review Microsoft 365 audit records for unusual mail or file access, downloads, forwarding, inbox or transport rules, delegated mailbox permissions, and related resource activity. Preserve evidence, then have an appropriately authorized responder remove confirmed unauthorized credentials, grants, owners, assignments, and identities. Additional recommendations Threat actor misuse of AI accelerates risk across enterprise environments by amplifying existing threats such as exploitation of vulnerabilities, phishing, malware threats, and insider activity. To help organizations stay ahead of AI-enabled threat activity, Microsoft has introduced the Security Dashboard for AI . The dashboard provides users with a unified view of AI security posture by aggregating security, identity, and data risk across Microsoft Defender , Microsoft Entra , and Microsoft Purview . This allows organizations to understand what AI assets exist in their environment, recognize emerging risk patterns, and prioritize governance and security across AI agents, applications, and platforms. To learn more about the Microsoft Security Dashboard for AI see: Assess your organization’s AI risk with Microsoft Security Dashboard for AI (Preview) . Enable threat protection for AI services in Microsoft Defender for Cloud to identify threats to generative AI applications in real time and for assistance in responding to security issues. Apply least privilege to multi-tenant application permissions and consent grants. Monitor credential additions, privilege assignments, and anomalous app-only activity, especially to applications with high privileged permissions and scopes. Verify that vendor credential rotation and any tenant-level remediation eliminated remaining unauthorized access. Assess the operational effect on backup and restore workflows and follow current ConnectWise restoration guidance. Microsoft Defender XDR detections Microsoft Defender XDR customers can refer to the list of applicable detections below. Microsoft Defender XDR coordinates detection, prevention, investigation, and response across endpoints, identities, email, and apps to provide integrated protection against attacks like the threat discussed in this blog. Customers with provisioned access can also use Microsoft Security Copilot in Microsoft Defender to investigate and respond to incidents, hunt for threats, and protect their organization with relevant threat intelligence. Tactic Observed activity Microsoft Defender coverage (Alert title) Discovery Unusual behavior attributes were observed from Graph API activity originating from associated ConnectWise Application. Unusual Microsoft Graph activity associated with Compromised ConnectWise Application Privilege Escalation Persistence Initial Access/Valid Accounts ConnectWise Management Application directly granted itself the Global Administrator role through the Add member to role operation, with no prior Global Administrator self-assignment observed for the same application in the preceding 7 days. Application self-assigned Global Administrator role Discovery Graph API activity for the user originated from an active, production Microsoft Threat Intelligence Center IP indicator. Graph API activity from a Microsoft threat intelligence IP address Valid Accounts A user sign-in from a nation-state threat actor infrastructure has been detected from this account. A threat actor might have compromised the user account to gain unauthorized access and conducted other malicious activities in your system. Investigate promptly to mitigate security risks. Suspicious sign-in from verified nation-state threat actor infrastructure Steal Application Access Token A sign-in was observed from a known threat actor IP address. We recommend promptly investigating this alert, as a threat actor might already be using the stolen credentials to move laterally in the network. Malicious sign-in from known threat actor IP address Microsoft Defender for Cloud Apps detections Tactic Observed activity Microsoft Defender coverage (Alert title) Persistence An application or service principal was granted a highly privileged app role. Suspicious addition of app role assignments to service principal Collection High-volume mailbox access by an OAuth app after a suspicious role grant. Suspicious mail access activity by OAuth application following role assignment Collection A suspicious OAuth app that was added recently started accessing the Teams Messages folder using an email client. Newly added OAuth application accessing Teams Messages folder via email client Credential Access An OAuth application activity from an uncommonly visited ISP has been observed, indicating potential suspicious behavior. OAuth application activity from an uncommonly visited ISP Exfiltration OAuth applications seen performing extensive Microsoft Graph SharePoint enumeration activities shortly after application creation or modification events Suspicious OAuth application created from a risky user context performing graph SharePoint enumeration Privilege Escalation Risky permissions that enable user to act as other entities or escalate to Global Admin provided to Service Principal High-privilege application roles assigned to a service principal Persistence A service principal added an application role assignment to itself Suspicious addition of application role assignments by service principal to itself Microsoft Security Copilot Security Copilot customers can use the standalone experience to create their own prompts or run the following prebuilt promptbooks to automate incident response or investigation tasks related to this threat: Incident investigation Threat actor profile Threat Intelligence 360 report based on MDTI article Note that some promptbooks require access to plugins for Microsoft products such as Microsoft Defender XDR or Microsoft Sentinel. Threat intelligence reports Microsoft customers can use the following reports in Microsoft products to get the most up-to-date information about the threat actor, malicious activity, and techniques discussed in this blog. These reports provide intelligence, protection information, and recommended actions to prevent, mitigate, or respond to associated threats found in customer environments. Microsoft Defender XDR Threat analytics Activity Profile: ConnectWise Cloud Backup credential abuse: assessment and response guidance Indicators of compromise (IOC) Indicator Type Description 144.172.64[.]128 IP These IPs were seen performing Sign-ins and Graph API activity in customer environments of ConnectWise apps. 144.172.64[.]99 IP 144.172.64[.]60 IP 187.15.88[.]186 187.15.90[.]217 187.15.89[.]186 IP These IPs were seen accessing the Graph API via the compromised apps. However, since they are VPN IPs, it is transient and relevant for investigation on October 15 and 16 in context with compromised applications. Python-urllib/3.12 User Agent These user agents were seen performing Sign-ins and Graph API activity on customer environments using ConnectWise apps. python-requests/2.31.0 User Agent python-requests/2.34.2 User Agent curl/7.88.1 User Agent azure-toolkit/1.0 User Agent Advanced hunting NOTE : The following sample queries let you search for a week’s worth of events. To explore up to 30 days’ worth of raw data to inspect events in your network and locate potential indicators related to this campaign for more than a week, go to the Advanced Hunting page > Query tab, select the calendar dropdown menu to update your query to hunt for the Last 30 days . Microsoft Defender XDR advanced hunting 1- OAuthAppInfo → Is the affected app present, enabled, and what permissions does it hold? Start with OAuthAppInfo to determine whether any of the affected ConnectWise applications are present in the tenant and understand the access they have been granted. The query identifies the application and its tenant-specific service principal, whether it is enabled, its privilege level, consent information, and the individual permissions assigned to it. This establishes the customer’s potential exposure and gives investigators the ServicePrincipalId needed for further hunting. A match does not mean the application was abused, only that it is present and potentially had access, so the next step is to determine whether the service principal was actually used. Run query let ConnectWiseApps = dynamic([ "506e08f9-6e9a-4da4-942b-a099a03644ae", // ConnectWise Cloud Backup "24205314-2b89-4e07-a2a4-579e898a5640", // ConnectWise - MS Teams "0de14c77-b9b0-4137-9360-34878a929827", // ConnectWise - MS Graph "c921256f-04a7-44e8-9b2a-69c33929ba19" // SkyKick Partner Portal ]); OAuthAppInfo | where OAuthAppId in (ConnectWiseApps) | mv-expand Permission = Permissions | extend PermissionName = tostring(Permission.PermissionName), TargetApp = tostring(Permission.TargetAppDisplayName), TargetAppId = tostring(Permission.TargetAppId), PermissionType = tostring(Permission.PermissionType), PermissionPrivilegeLevel = tostring(Permission.PrivilegeLevel), UsageStatus = tostring(Permission.UsageStatus) | project AppName, OAuthAppId, ServicePrincipalId, AppStatus, PrivilegeLevel, IsAdminConsented, PermissionName, PermissionType, PermissionPrivilegeLevel, TargetApp, TargetAppId, UsageStatus | order by AppName asc, PermissionPrivilegeLevel desc 2 – EntraIdSpnSignInEvents + GraphAPIAuditEvents → Did the service principal authenticate, and what Microsoft Graph activity followed? Use this query to investigate service-principal sign-ins and Microsoft Graph API activity associated with the identified ConnectWise applications and suspicious IP addresses, starting October 13, 2026. The query combines both event types into a chronological view, helping defenders identify suspicious authentication and related Graph operations, including potential credential changes, privilege modifications, and unusual resource access. Remove the IP filter for broader hunting. Results require further correlation, as authentication alone does not establish compromise. Run query let Apps = dynamic([ "506e08f9-6e9a-4da4-942b-a099a03644ae", "24205314-2b89-4e07-a2a4-579e898a5640", "0de14c77-b9b0-4137-9360-34878a929827", "c921256f-04a7-44e8-9b2a-69c33929ba19" ]); let IPs = dynamic(["144.172.64.60", "144.172.64.99", "144.172.64.128"]); union kind=outer (EntraIdSpnSignInEvents | extend EventType = "Sign-in"), (GraphAPIAuditEvents | extend EventType = "Graph API", IPAddress = IpAddress) | where Timestamp >= datetime(2026-10-13) | where ApplicationId in (Apps) | where IPAddress in (IPs) // Comment out for broader hunting | project-away IpAddress | order by Timestamp asc Sentinel hunting queries 1-SigninLogs → Did a service principal authenticate, from where, and against what resource? Use SigninLogs to determine whether an affected application identity actually authenticated. This moves the investigation from potential exposure to observed authentication, allowing defenders to examine the application and service principal alongside the source IP address, geographic information, authentication result, and resource being accessed. Investigators should evaluate these sign-ins against the application’s expected activity and look for unusual source infrastructure, resources, or authentication patterns before pivoting into subsequent Graph activity. Run query let IPIndicators = dynamic([ "144.172.64.60", // IP Indicator "144.172.64.99", // IP Indicator "144.172.64.128" // IP Indicator ]); let ConnectWiseApps = dynamic([ "506e08f9-6e9a-4da4-942b-a099a03644ae", // ConnectWise Cloud Backup "24205314-2b89-4e07-a2a4-579e898a5640", // ConnectWise - MS Teams "0de14c77-b9b0-4137-9360-34878a929827", // ConnectWise - MS Graph "c921256f-04a7-44e8-9b2a-69c33929ba19" // SkyKick Partner Portal ]); SigninLogs | where TimeGenerated >= datetime(2026-10-13) | where AppId in (ConnectWiseApps) //| where IPAddress in (IPIndicators) // Comment out to review all activity from these applications | project TimeGenerated, AppId, ServicePrincipalName, ResourceDisplayName, ResourceId, IPAddress, CorrelationId | order by TimeGenerated asc 2 – MicrosoftGraphActivityLogs → What observable Graph API activity followed? Use MicrosoftGraphActivityLogs to investigate observable Microsoft Graph activity following authentication. This query allows defenders to pivot on the affected ApplicationId or tenant-specific ServicePrincipalId and examine details such as the request URI, HTTP method, response status, scopes, source IP address, and target workload. This helps establish what Graph activity occurred after the service principal authenticated and provides additional context around the resources the application attempted to access. Importantly, the absence of results should not be treated as confirmation that no access occurred; Graph API telemetry should be considered alongside the application permissions and service principal authentication activity identified in the previous hunting steps. Run query let IPIndicators = dynamic([ "144.172.64.60", // IP Indicator "144.172.64.99", // IP Indicator "144.172.64.128" // IP Indicator ]); let ConnectWiseApps = dynamic([ "506e08f9-6e9a-4da4-942b-a099a03644ae", // ConnectWise Cloud Backup "24205314-2b89-4e07-a2a4-579e898a5640", // ConnectWise - MS Teams "0de14c77-b9b0-4137-9360-34878a929827", // ConnectWise - MS Graph "c921256f-04a7-44e8-9b2a-69c33929ba19" // SkyKick Partner Portal ]); MicrosoftGraphActivityLogs | where TimeGenerated >= datetime(2026-10-13) | where AppId in (ConnectWiseApps) | where IPAddress in (IPIndicators) // Comment out to review all Graph activity from these applications | project TimeGenerated, AppId, IPAddress, RequestMethod, RequestUri, ResponseStatusCode, Scopes, ClientRequestId, OperationId, RequestId | order by TimeGenerated asc MITRE ATT&CK Techniques observed This threat has exhibited use of the following attack techniques. T1098.001 Account Manipulation: Additional Cloud Credentials | Addition or modification of application credentials. article.raw_text: Two critical RCEs in PHP core Cisco Talos is tracking the disclosure of two unauthenticated remote code execution (RCE) flaws in PHP core, dubbed “php2shell”, triggered by a plain HTTP request and exploitable before any application code runs, affecting every PHP build since 5.4. Based on the entities involved in the disclosure, artificial Cisco Talos is tracking the disclosure of two unauthenticated remote code execution (RCE) flaws in PHP core, dubbed “php2shell”, triggered by a plain HTTP request and exploitable before any application code runs, affecting every PHP build since 5.4. Based on the entities involved in the disclosure, artificial intelligence and associated technologies played a key role in the discovery of these vulnerabilities — yet another example of how these technologies are forcing change across the landscape, most notably on patching processes for organizations because of the wave of vulnerabilities being disclosed. Cisco customers are covered with the Cisco Talos Network Intrusion Prevention (SNORT®) signatures 67359 and 67360. These rules are also available in the Community Ruleset for open-source customers. Please refer to the following recommendations, detection, and coverage guidance for more information. Details CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 are both critical vulnerabilities with a CVSS v4.0 score of 9.2. CVE-2026-109618 occurs when out-of-memory handling interrupts PHP while internal request data is only partially initialized. Request cleanup may then treat invalid data as valid. CVE-2026-109619 occurs when a stale internal state is reused after its backing memory has already been freed, before normal initialization resets it. Impact The potential blast radius is enormous and extends across the PHP ecosystem. The vulnerability sits in PHP core, so applications running affected versions — including WordPress, Drupal, Magento, Shopware, WooCommerce, and Laravel, plus PHP sites hosted through cPanel or Plesk — may be exposed. Note that many older branches will no longer receive fixes, so customers are urged to upgrade to a supported version as soon as possible. Talos regularly investigates threat actor exploitation of vulnerabilities. State-sponsored and affiliated threat actors, as well as ransomware and other financially motivated groups, all employ tactics to exploit RCE. Talos assesses that all industries running PHP applications are at risk for exploitation if systems remain unpatched. PHP 8.1 and older are end of life (EOL), and PHP 8.2 security support ends Dec. 31, 2026. Talos’ initial estimates based on open-source intelligence show a significant corpus of PHP systems that will not receive a patch (~50%). If your organization is running PHP 8.1 or older, Talos very strongly advises immediate update to PHP 8.2 or later. There is no patch for PHP 8.1 or older. Talos is actively monitoring the impact of these CVEs and has not seen them being exploited in the wild yet (as of October 21, 2026 14:00 UTC/10:00 a.m. ET). Recommendations and detection guidance Talos strongly recommends all PHP users to upgrade to the available fixed releases . There are no intermediate or temporary controls that provide comprehensive protection; however, PHP advises that the following measure may reduce exposure to specific attack paths: CVE-2026-109618 Set memory_limit=-1, preferably in a way applications can't override, such as php_admin_value in the FPM pool or Apache configuration, and check that no pool, directory or application setting puts a finite limit back. This removes the controllable PHP memory limit failure, but an underlying allocation failure can still reach the vulnerable path. Set a low post_max_size. For applications that don't require file uploads, set post_max_size = 8M. If file uploads are necessary, set post_max_size = 32M. Keep upload_max_filesize below post_max_size. Consider enforcing limits at the web server or proxy level for decoded request size, input field count, multipart part count, header count, and nesting depth. These limits must also cover requests without a usable Content-Length. Use a container or cgroup limit as an availability boundary, preferably with a policy that kills only the affected worker. Do not substitute RLIMIT_AS or RLIMIT_DATA, as these can cause the vulnerable allocation failure. CVE-2026-109619 Set session.upload_progress.enabled=0 and restart every worker. Use php.ini, an FPM pool, or server configuration that applies before request parsing. Do not rely on ini_set() or FPM .user.ini. This blocks the confirmed session paths but not other variants. On PHP 8.5, set fatal_error_backtraces=0 and restart every worker. This blocks the confirmed fatal backtrace path only. Remove invalid or deprecated settings applied per request that emit diagnostics before initialization. Hiding diagnostics with error_reporting, display_errors, or @ does not help. Fix attacker-reachable fatal errors and execution timeouts, including failures in callbacks, upload or import processing, and cleanup. This is another vulnerability that owes its origin to AI and its associated technologies. As we move through 2026, the wave of vulnerabilities and related patches is building. Talos advises organizations to work on a triaged process for prioritizing vulnerabilities with a specific focus on public-facing systems and vulnerabilities that are under active exploitation. The glaring need to prioritize vulnerabilities along with a streamlined process for rolling out patching strongly indicates that the historic trend of “baking in” patches before deployment is not going to survive the AI era. The true impact of this vulnerability will take time to evaluate. These types of vulnerabilities that impact core technologies tend to cascade into other platforms and applications as they evaluate impact and provide associated patching, harkening back to the waves of exploitation that we saw after Log4J. Coverage SNORT® SIDs covering these vulnerabilities for subscribers: 67359, 67360. Free community rules are live through our Community Ruleset . Talos would like to highlight the efforts of Ankur Tyagi, Dalton Schaadt, Brandon Stultz and Matt Killion for providing emergency coverage and mitigations for these threats.

objectives.title: Inventory exposure to the affected product
objectives.falsification_criterion: If zero internet-facing assets run a vulnerable build of the affected product, the external-exploitation hypothesis is disproven for CVE-2026-107617.
objectives.suggested_query: asset_inventory | where product == 'the affected product' and exposure == 'internet' and version in (vulnerable_versions)

objectives.title: Hunt for exploit attempts at the edge
objectives.falsification_criterion: If WAF / firewall / IDS show no exploit-signature hits for CVE-2026-107617 in the last 30 days, in-the-wild exploitation against us is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: edge_logs | where signature contains 'CVE' or uri matches /exploit-pattern-for-CVE-2026-107617/ | summarize count() by src_ip, dst_host

objectives.title: Patch-status correlation
objectives.falsification_criterion: If MDM / patch-management shows 100% deployment of the CVE-2026-107617 fix across exposed hosts, the hypothesis is disproven by remediation.
objectives.suggested_query: patch_state | where kb in (fixes_for('CVE-2026-107617')) | summarize coverage = avg(installed) by host_role

objectives.title: Post-exploit web-shell sweep
objectives.falsification_criterion: If a sweep of webroots and IIS/Apache process trees finds no anomalous children (cmd, powershell, /bin/sh) on the affected product hosts, post-exploit foothold is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: process | where parent in ('w3wp.exe','httpd','nginx','java') and child in ('cmd.exe','powershell.exe','/bin/sh','/bin/bash')

objectives.title: Honeypot / canary check
objectives.falsification_criterion: If exposed canary instances of the same product show no probing or exploitation telemetry, opportunistic mass-exploitation against the org is unlikely.
objectives.suggested_query: canary_events | where product == '<product>' | where event_type in ('probe','exploit') | summarize by src_ip

hypotheses.title: Outbound C2 beaconing to reported infrastructure
hypotheses.statement: Hosts in the estate are beaconing to the command-and-control infrastructure reported in this article (domains, IPs, TLS fingerprints, or RMM tooling).
hypotheses.rationale: Archetype 'c2_beacon' selected based on CVEs cited: CVE-2026-107617, CVE-2026-97858, CVE-2026-105664; vectors: phishing, exploit, vpn-edge.

objectives.title: DNS resolution sweep for published C2 domains
objectives.falsification_criterion: If recursive DNS logs show zero resolutions for the IOC domains in the last 90 days, active beaconing is disproven.
objectives.suggested_query: dns | where query in ('eseecloud.app','www.cisa.gov') | summarize count() by client_ip

objectives.title: Egress connections to published C2 IPs
objectives.falsification_criterion: If proxy / firewall egress logs show no connections to the IOC IPs or matching ASNs, network-level C2 is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: egress | where dst_ip in ('the published C2 IPs') | summarize bytes_out = sum(bytes_sent) by src_ip

objectives.title: Beacon periodicity / jitter analysis
objectives.falsification_criterion: If beacon-style periodic outbound connections (low jitter, small payloads) to uncategorised destinations are absent, covert C2 is unlikely.
objectives.suggested_query: conn | summarize stddev_interval = stdev(diff(ts)), count() by src_ip, dst_host | where count() > 50 and stddev_interval < 5s

objectives.title: TLS / JA3 fingerprint pivot
objectives.falsification_criterion: If JA3/JA3S fingerprints associated with the reported family are absent in TLS telemetry, encrypted C2 attribution is weakened.
objectives.suggested_query: tls | where ja3 in (ti_lookup('family','ja3')) | summarize by src_ip, sni

objectives.title: Remote-monitoring tooling abuse check
objectives.falsification_criterion: If unmanaged AnyDesk / TeamViewer / ScreenConnect / Atera installs are absent, RMM-based C2 is disproven.
objectives.suggested_query: process | where name in ('anydesk.exe','teamviewer.exe','screenconnect.exe','atera*.exe') and signer != 'corp_managed'

hypotheses.title: Identity compromise of privileged users
hypotheses.statement: Privileged identities have been compromised through phishing, MFA fatigue, help-desk social engineering, or OAuth illicit-consent grants.
hypotheses.rationale: Archetype 'identity_compromise' selected based on CVEs cited: CVE-2026-107617, CVE-2026-97858, CVE-2026-105664; vectors: phishing, exploit, vpn-edge.

objectives.title: Impossible-travel / atypical sign-ins
objectives.falsification_criterion: If Entra ID / Okta risky-sign-in detections show no impossible-travel hits on privileged identities, account compromise is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: signin | where risk_level in ('high','medium') and user in (privileged_users) | summarize by country, ip

objectives.title: MFA-fatigue / push-bombing
objectives.falsification_criterion: If MFA telemetry shows no bursts of denied pushes followed by a successful one for the same user, MFA-fatigue compromise is disproven.
objectives.suggested_query: mfa | summarize denies = countif(result=='deny'), accepts = countif(result=='accept') by user, bin(ts,1h) | where denies > 5 and accepts > 0

objectives.title: Help-desk social-engineering pivot
objectives.falsification_criterion: If ticketing / call-recording shows no recent password-reset or MFA-reset requests for privileged users without proper verification, help-desk vector is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: tickets | where action in ('password_reset','mfa_reset') and target in (privileged_users) | join (verifications) on ticket_id

objectives.title: OAuth illicit-consent grants
objectives.falsification_criterion: If Entra/Workspace audit logs show no recently consented third-party apps with high-impact scopes, OAuth abuse is disproven.
objectives.suggested_query: audit | where action == 'Consent to application' and scopes contains 'Mail.Read' or 'files.read.all'

article.title: Kiloview E3 NDI Encoder
article.summary: View CSAF Summary Successful exploitation of this these vulnerabilities could allow an attacker to fully compromise the device. The following versions of Kiloview E3 NDI Encoder are affected: E3 Firmware CVSS Vendor Equipment v3 9.9 Kiloview E3 Firmware 6 Vulnerabilities Improper Neutralization of Special Elements used in an OS Command ('OS Command Injection'), Missing Authentication for Critical Function, Insufficient Session Expiration, Improper Limitation of a Pathname to a Restricted Directory ('Path Traversal'), NULL Pointer Dereference, Use of Hard-coded Credentials Background Critical Infrastructure Sectors: Communications, Information Technology Countries/Areas Deployed: Worldwide Company Headquarters Location: China Vulnerabilities Expand All + CVE-2026-109122 The network management service on affected Kiloview E3 NDI encoder firmware fails to sanitize one field used when configuring static routes via the web management API. An authenticated web user with permission to configure static routes can exploit this to execute arbitrary operating system commands as root, and the malicious configuration persists across reboots. Successful exploitation could result in full device compromise, including exposure of stored credentials and cryptographic material. Read More 1 Affected Product Kiloview E3 Firmware: Product Status: known_affected Remediations Mitigation KiloView recommends users update to V1.30: https://www.kiloview.com/en/download/e3-firmware-downloadlatest-12/ Add

these vulnerabilities to CISA. Recommended Practices CISA recommends users take defensive measures to minimize the risk of exploitation of these vulnerabilities. Minimize network exposure for all control system devices and/or systems, ensuring they are not accessible from the internet . Locate control system networks and remote devices behind firewalls and isolating them from business networks. When remote access is required, use more secure methods, such as Virtual Private Networks (VPNs), recognizing VPNs may have vulnerabilities and should be updated to the most current version available. Also recognize VPN is only as secure as the connected devices. CISA reminds organizations to perform proper impact analysis and risk assessment prior to deploying defensive measures. CISA also provides a section for control systems security recommended practices on the ICS webpage on cisa.gov/ics . Several CISA products detailing cyber defense best practices are available for reading and download, including Improving Industrial Control Systems Cybersecurity with Defense-in-Depth Strategies . CISA encourages organizations to implement recommended cybersecurity strategies for proactive defense of ICS assets . Additional mitigation guidance and recommended practices are publicly available on the ICS webpage at cisa.gov/ics in the technical information paper, ICS-TIP-12-146-01B--Targeted Cyber Intrusion Detection and Mitigation Strategies . Organizations observing suspected malicious activity should follow established internal procedures and report findings to CISA for tracking and correlation against other incidents. CISA also recommends users take the following measures to protect themselves from social engineering attacks: Do not click web links or open attachments in unsolicited email messages. Refer to Recognizing and Avoiding Email Scams for more information on avoiding email scams. Refer to Avoiding Social Engineering and Phishing Attacks for more information on social engineering attacks. No known public exploitation specifically targeting these vulnerabilities has been reported to CISA at this time.
