article.title: Compromised eMudhra intermediate certificates
article.summary: Cisco Talos is aware of eight intermediate certificates belonging to the intermediate certificate authority, eMudhra.
article.raw_text: Compromised eMudhra intermediate certificates Cisco Talos is aware of eight intermediate certificates belonging to the intermediate certificate authority, eMudhra. Cisco Talos is aware of eight intermediate certificates belonging to the intermediate certificate authority, eMudhra . Rather than possessing the mandatory 384 bits of pseudo-random security, several private keys evaluated single-digit and double-digit integers. This misconfiguration allows an attacker with the private key of any of the compromised intermediate CAs to impersonate any website or service. Six of the TLS certificates, trusted by Chrome, Mozilla, and Apple have been blocked by these vendors already. Two other certificates, used for codesigning by Microsoft, have also been blocked. Talos expects there will be additional patches available across a variety of technologies as software applications work to remediate the certificates’ exposure. Following the disclosure, eMudhra has revoked the compromised certificates and stopped issuing new certificates under its G3 root. Compromise details The cause of this issue, originated during an April 30, 2025 key generation activity conducted by eMudhra under its emSign Root TLS CA - G3 and cross-signed Comodo AAA Certificate Services. During a key generation ceremony for 24 subordinate CAs, a flaw in eMudhra’s key generation process created a second set of weak P-384 keys during a wrap/unwrap step. Those keys were mistakenly used for eight intermediate CA certificates. This flaw took the encryption from 384 bytes of entropy down to 3 – 8, making recovering the private keys trivial. The following are the impacted certificates, as illustrated in Mozilla’s bug report : EM EV TLS CA - G3B (eMudhra BV), CCADB A012304 SHA-256 E7568FE6E12331F4FD7DE61DA4C7559D0F8EB192A218D4741A3BA75184333838 serial c7c41efe92d825f05eae841a4a82c1, issuer emSign Root TLS CA - G3 EM OV TLS CA - G3B (eMudhra BV), CCADB A012308 SHA-256 98B896625C0C230ADEEC3EB2CF6AAD5001ECF9156A68644E82374CE5833BC25B serial 6cada367fb1c100088120ea202d568, issuer emSign Root TLS CA - G3 EM DV TLS CA - G3B (eMudhra BV), CCADB A012302 SHA-256 42C4ACCD12C4F59597925E1A08A7A90102608543809308D50EC427E118BA1493 serial a4aee678f23362b4c0e460b772f214, issuer emSign Root TLS CA - G3 EM EV TLS CA - G3C (eMudhra Inc), CCADB A012296 SHA-256 432EC25F0D28DE9006D97BF752F17BBB2CD41F669933FCB072D9A1148D0261F3 serial 8009928a64107601af05fa2f19f109, issuer emSign Root TLS CA - G3 EM OV TLS CA - G3C (eMudhra Inc), CCADB A012300 SHA-256 CB6E15165AC802E9B3F993F16C25D41F4E81C21EBDE71AE1B012AC00BF9C7C3F serial 296926c227a3a1526392b19482a504, issuer emSign Root TLS CA - G3 EM DV TLS CA - G3C (eMudhra Inc), CCADB A012294 SHA-256 0164D7CEAE5BB909C272AF151FF44B1177AE9B47D9424B94F1D9558C30934D19 serial 588b2e3c2bb8cda13e1a1209254321, issuer emSign Root TLS CA - G3 EM OV CS CA - G3B (eMudhra BV), CCADB A012306 SHA-256 9E39DE2881273ACC225A149C72BA3E0F51424963669AB633EE1DC7DF5DB067B4 serial 7818933f8f85b4619a2b35fba83d0a, issuer emSign Root CS CA - G3 EM OV CS CA - G3C (eMudhra Inc), CCADB A012298 SHA-256 4B2460A466F95FD40113BCDCCA2CEB29B3B093921DE45474DA7DF48874C630B1 serial 544b7f922c31ae220a4a922916f6e6, issuer emSign Root CS CA - G3 CVE-2026-111943 Unlike languages that defer entirely to external dynamic system libraries (like OpenSSL), the Go programming runtime implements its own X.509 chain verification engine in the standard library (crypto/x509). While Go usually queries platform certificates, several platforms or static container environments rely on embedded or legacy root certificate pools where certificate revocations are ignored. To eliminate exploitation across the entire cloud-native ecosystem including Docker, Kubernetes, Terraform, and Prometheus, the Go team designated the compromised certificates as a vulnerability, CVE-2026-111943, and released Go versions 1.27.3 and 1.26.10. The fixed versions filter out chains containingthe SHA-256 hashes of the SubjectPublicKeyInfo (SPKI) for all eight compromised eMudhra intermediate certificates. Impact These compromised certificates could allow adversaries to impersonate servers and intercept or modify traffic. The impact of their exposure is far more than just web browsers. Other programs that check for TLS certificates might still be impacted since they may not check revocation lists. One clear example is related to virtual private networks (VPNs); these technologies will likely require software updates to mitigate the issue. Based on this guidance, Talos strongly recommends users update software using and handling TLS certificates as fixes become available. Talos is actively monitoring the impact of these compromised certificates and has not seen any malicious incidents involving them in the wild yet (as of October 21, 2026 14:00 UTC / 10:00 a.m. ET). Significance of this breach Public key infrastructure relies on trust being delegated through certificate chains: root CAs authorize intermediate CAs, which can issue certificates within the scope of their authority. An attacker who obtains an intermediate CA’s private key may be able to issue fraudulent certificates that clients accept, subject to the intermediate certificate’s constraints and each client’s validation controls. In this incident, six compromised intermediates were for TLS and two were for code signing. For TLS, an attacker able to intercept or redirect a connection could use a fraudulent certificate to impersonate a server and potentially read or modify traffic if the client still trusts the affected key and no applicable protection blocks it. Protections such as revocation, key distrust, certificate transparency enforcement, and certificate pinning can prevent or expose such an attack. Browser vendors have blocked the affected TLS keys, but other applications may rely on separate trust stores or validation paths: Enterprise infrastructure and VPNs Organizations should assess TLS-using software and appliances, including proxies, reverse load balancers, VPN clients, and gateways. Exposure depends on the certificate chain being validated and the trust store and revocation behavior in use. A stale or separately managed trust store may need an application, operating-system, firmware, or trust-bundle update; verify the required action for each product. Software supply chains and CI/CD Build runners and package managers may be exposed if they fetch content over TLS while still trusting an affected key and an attacker can intercept the connection. A fraudulent TLS certificate could enable registry impersonation, but it would not by itself bypass separate package integrity checks, such as lockfile hashes, checksums, signatures, or provenance controls. Assess the actual package-manager configuration and dependency path. Industrial IoT and embedded systems Review devices that use bundled or independently managed CA stores, especially where certificate revocation or trust-store updates may be limited. Some devices may require a vendor update or compensating control, but the necessary action depends on each device’s validation and update mechanisms. Talos recommends updating affected software and trust stores as vendor fixes become available. Coverage The following SNORT® SIDs provide coverage for this threat: 67363 - 67374. Talos would like to highlight the efforts of Chris Morrison for providing emergency coverage and mitigations for this threat.

article.raw_text: Patch Tuesday - October 2026 Microsoft is publishing 1,413 own-product vulnerabilities on October 2026 Patch Tuesday , including 1,102 vulnerabilities in Windows. Anyone who enjoyed last month’s record-setting Patch Tuesday will love the October 2026 edition, because it’s much bigger still. As Rapid7 has noted over the course of 2026, there is every reason to suppose that vulnerability volumes will continue to rise. Microsoft is aware of exploitation in the wild for just one of the vulnerabilities published today, as well as public disclosure for two others. Windows Shell: zero-day security feature bypass The Windows Shell is Microsoft’s term for the GUI interaction logic for the entire OS provided by explorer.exe and associated libraries and APIs, and for the second time this year , the Windows Shell is the site of an exploited-in-the-wild zero-day vulnerability. Today’s specimen is CVE-2026-96951 . Once again, the immediate prize for an attacker is a Mark of the Web (MOTW) bypass. What this means is that Windows won’t provide the user with a dialog explaining that Windows protected their PC, because in this case, it didn’t. Exploitation requires that a user opens a specially crafted malicious file or visits an attacker-controlled site, so the evergreen advice about being careful what you click remains valid. Fans of vintage operating systems should note that Windows Server 2012 doesn’t receive a patch, although Server 2012 R2 does. The advisory acknowledges reporters from multiple organizations, although none from within Microsoft. The vulnerability also affected Microsoft’s Outlook.com cloud services, although Outlook.com was patched in a build dated several weeks ago. .NET Framework: zero-day security feature bypass Microsoft is aware of some level of public disclosure of CVE-2026-108398 , a .NET Framework security feature bypass. Exploitation requires an attacker with an existing foothold to register a malicious .NET assembly for loading by a protected process, bypassing Windows Defender Application Control (WDAC) enforcement. Microsoft rebranded WDAC as App Control for Business several years ago, so you may know it under its new name. The Microsoft Learn page for Application Control for Windows points out that “your organization's data is one of its most valuable assets... and threat actors want it”, and this is, of course, correct. The patch presumably removes an attacker-controlled location from the list of places .NET Framework searches for registered assemblies, which are typically contained within DLLs and executables. If any further indications were needed that vulnerability volumes are increasing industry-wide, this is only the second month that Microsoft has published vulnerabilities with six-digit CVE numbers, but these extra-large CVEs will seem unremarkable from now on. Outlook: multiple no-interaction RCEs The sheer volume of vulnerabilities in recent Patch Tuesday releases can easily include several examples of potentially concerning vulnerabilities, each of which might have been more remarkable in its own right back when volumes were lower. Today, Microsoft has published five separate remote code execution vulnerabilities in Outlook where the preview pane is a vector, meaning that simply scrolling past an email in the Outlook reading pane would be sufficient to trigger exploitation. Worse still, Outlook might helpfully display the preview without any user interaction at all. All five of CVE-2026-70242 , CVE-2026-97749 , CVE-2026-97016 , CVE-2026-88156 , and CVE-2026-70291 receive fixes in the same patches. No-interaction Outlook preview pane vulnerabilities can sometimes feature prominently in state-backed actor campaigns, with CVE-2023-23397 as a prominent example in this category . Edge: security updates unclear In September 2026, Microsoft did not appear to publish any desktop browser security advisories between the start of the month and Patch Tuesday. In October, a slightly different approach has emerged: several recent entries in the Edge security updates release notes mention new versions of Edge which incorporate the latest updates from the Chromium project, but without detailing which vulnerabilities have been fixed, stating instead, “CVE's will be added as soon as available,” and directing readers to the Security Update Guide (SUG). At the time of writing, the SUG lists a total of zero vulnerabilities addressed in Edge in the first 13 days of October, and the “CVE’s added soon” message has been up for over a week. As a result, defenders have no obvious way of knowing which recent vulnerabilities Microsoft has addressed in Edge. Microsoft lifecycle update In Microsoft product lifecycle news, today sees Windows 11 24H2 Home & Pro reach end of servicing, while Windows Server 2022 moves to extended support, with free critical security updates continuing but no further feature development. Also this month, the final curtain falls for Windows Server 2012 and 2012 R2 with the expiry of the third and final year of cash-for-updates Extended Security Update (ESU) program for these aging workhorses. Microsoft lists the end of ESU Year 3 on October 14, 2026, in both cases. Microsoft has a long history of providing at least some security patches for products beyond the end of support, with Server 2008 being a case in point, but the time to move past Server 2012 is now. Office 2021 also moves into retirement on October 14; this includes the Long-Term Servicing Channel , with no ESU available in that case. Also on October 15, 2026, Exchange Server 2016 and Exchange Server 2019 finally join the “no ESU” club, after two previous six-month reprieves. Microsoft seems to really mean it this time, since any future Exchange Server CVEs released by MSRC will stop mentioning Exchange 2016 and 2019. However, Microsoft points out that a lack of warnings does not mean those unsupported versions are not vulnerable to future security issues. Summary charts

article.title: Siemens Industrial Edge App Publisher
article.summary: View CSAF Summary The Industrial Edge App Publisher contains a vulnerability chain involving improper certificate validation and the rendering of unescaped data from backend responses. These issues can be combined to allow an attacker on the network to impersonate the management server and execute arbitrary code (RCE) on the local machine through Node.js integration. Siemens has released an update for the Industrial Edge App Publisher and recommends to update to the latest version. The following versions of Siemens Industrial Edge App Publisher are affected: Industrial Edge App Publisher vers:intdot/ CVSS Vendor Equipment v3 8.3 Siemens Industrial Edge App Publisher 2 Vulnerabilities Improper Certificate Validation, Improper Neutralization of Input During Web Page Generation ('Cross-site Scripting') Background Critical Infrastructure Sectors: Critical Manufacturing, Transportation Systems, Energy, Healthcare and Public Health, Financial Services, Government Services and Facilities Countries/Areas Deployed: Worldwide Company Headquarters Location: Germany Vulnerabilities Expand All + CVE-2026-78556 The affected software does not properly validate the server certificate when initiating a TLS connection. This allows an attacker to intercept and relay communication (Man-in-the-Middle attack) and to spoof a trusted entity by interfering in the communication path between the client and the intended server. In order to operate the devices in a protected IT environment, Siemens recommends to configure the environment according to Siemens' operational guidelines for Industrial Security (Download: https://www.siemens.com/cert/operational-guidelines-industrial-security), and to follow the recommendations in the product manuals. Additional information on Industrial Security by Siemens can be found at: https://www.siemens.com/industrialsecurity Additional Resources For further inquiries on security vulnerabilities in Siemens products and solutions, please contact the Siemens ProductCERT: https://www.siemens.com/cert/advisories Terms of Use The use of Siemens Security Advisories is subject to the terms and conditions listed on: https://www.siemens.com/productcert/terms-of-use. Recommended Practices CISA recommends users take defensive measures to minimize the risk of exploitation of these vulnerabilities. Minimize network exposure for all control system devices and/or systems, ensuring they are not accessible from the internet . Locate control system networks and remote devices behind firewalls and isolating them from business networks. When remote access is required, use more secure methods, such as Virtual Private Networks (VPNs), recognizing VPNs may have vulnerabilities and should be updated to the most current version available. Also recognize VPN is only as secure as the connected devices. CISA reminds organizations to perform proper impact analysis and risk assessment prior to deploying defensive measures. CISA also provides a section for control systems security recommended practices on the ICS webpage on cisa.gov/ics . Several CISA products detailing cyber defense best practices are available for reading and download, including Improving Industrial Control Systems Cybersecurity with Defense-in-Depth Strategies . CISA encourages organizations to implement recommended cybersecurity strategies for proactive defense of ICS assets . Additional mitigation guidance and recommended practices are publicly available on the ICS webpage at cisa.gov/ics in the technical information paper, ICS-TIP-12-146-01B--Targeted Cyber Intrusion Detection and Mitigation Strategies . Organizations observing suspected malicious activity should follow established internal procedures and report findings to CISA for tracking and correlation against other incidents. article.title: I had plans for that second
article.summary: The Earth is speeding up, the leap second is being abolished, oh, and there's critical vulnerabilities in PHP.
article.raw_text: I had plans for that second The Earth is speeding up, the leap second is being abolished, oh, and there's critical vulnerabilities in PHP. Welcome to this week’s edition of the Threat Source newsletter. Here for the latest on the PHP vulnerabilities? Head on down to ‘The One Big Thing’. Talos has published a blog to explain what we know so far, and details the Snort coverage available, including rules in the Community Ruleset. But if you want a bit of levity, here’s what I wrote before everything kicked off yesterday: Ever feel like the world is moving too fast to keep up? Well, I bring you scientific proof that it’s not just you. For millions of years, the moon has been slowing down the Earth’s rotation. But over the past decade, we’ve been speeding up (I KNEW I was aging faster than before). Apparently, changes in the Earth’s core are involved (either that, or the 1978 Superman film was a documentary). This is all causing massive headaches for the people responsible for keeping time. They’re officially called “The International Bureau of Weights and Measures”, but I’m going to call them “The Time-Keepers”. For nerd reasons). The issue is that the atomic clocks that power so many of our systems, and the rotation of our planet, don’t always agree. Atomic clocks keep extremely consistent time, while each Earth day is rarely the same length as the next. Atomic timekeeping absolutely cannot stand that level of flexibility (have a watch of our “The Light We Keep” documentary to see the importance that accurate clocks have on critical infrastructure). To keep Coordinated Universal Time (UTC), which is based on atomic clocks, aligned with Earth’s rotation, we introduced a “leap second” in 1972. This system allows for an extra second to be added, or taken away, when we stray too far from atomic time. A few days ago, The Time-Keepers voted to officially abolish the leap second. Why? Well, there’s a few parts to it. For the past 54 years, we’ve never once had a second removed from our lives. They’ve always been added (27 of them to be precise). I myself have experienced 20 of these extra seconds. If I’d have known that, I’d have used them more wisely. Like thinking before saying, “Love you too!” to the post-person this morning. That added time, while it seems nice to have on the surface, can wreak havoc with our modern technology systems. In 2012, the extra second caused so much confusion that it crashed Reddit, among other systems. The recent speeding-up of the Earth’s rotation complicates things further. If we keep going at this rate, it could result in the world’s first ever “negative second”. If you thought our technology systems struggled with added time, there are a lot of sciency brains who are very worried about the impact of taking time away. One of those concerns being… it’s never been done before. So, what’s The Time-Keeper’s solution? Invent more time! Woooo. Starting next May, the leap second will be replaced with a "leap hour," allowing UTC to diverge from Earth's rotation by up to an hour before a correction is made. None of us will get to experience that extra hour in our lifetimes, but our Great, Great, Great, Great, Great, Great, Great, Great, Great, Great, Great grandchildren are going to have one hell of a party. For us current mortals, we’re all getting a little less time, and we’re hurtling through space a little faster. Happy Thursday! But I guess I do want to make the point that I’m glad the risk has been thoroughly assessed ahead of, ahem, time. The Time-Keepers have decided that the world’s infrastructure should not have to find out how it handles a missing second by collectively experiencing one. And I don’t even want to think about how all the AIs would cope with a negative second… There’s something here for incident response planning. “It’s never happened before” is an excellent reason to test whether you’re ready for it. Run the exercise. Find out which part of your plan depends on something that, in this scenario, is also broken. Preferably before an adversary gets to supervise the practical demonstration. Now, if only the Time-Keepers can abolish Daylight Savings Time next... The one big thing Two unauthenticated remote code execution (RCE) flaws were discovered in PHP, rocking the internet. Dubbed "php2shell" and triggered by a simple HTTP request, this vulnerability affects every build since 5.4. Talos assesses that all industries running PHP applications are at risk for exploitation if systems remain unpatched. Why do I care? PHP runs WordPress, Drupal, Magento, Shopware, WooCommerce, and many other ubiquitous internet staples, so the possible blast radius is enormous. Older branches are end of life (EOL) and will not receive patches; these could account for around 50% of use cases. So now what? Cisco customers are covered with the Cisco Talos Network Intrusion Prevention (SNORT®) signatures 67359 and 67360. If your organization is running PHP 8.1 or older, Talos very strongly advises immediate update to PHP 8.2 or later. There is no patch for PHP 8.1 or older. See the article for more specific coverage and detection guidance. See an interview with Nick Biasini on php2shell defense: Top security headlines of the week 'PHP2Shell' Bugs Signal Red Alert for Security Industry Security teams are scrambling to remediate two critical PHP vulnerabilities following leaked details and reports of exploitation attempts. ( Dark Reading ) I NC and The Gentlemen Ransomware Affiliates expose 8,257 AI messages SOCRadar has found seven exposed servers linked to INC and The Gentlemen ransomware affiliates, holding AI chats, stolen credentials and 46 encryptor builds. ( Hack Read ) T he AI hacking apocalypse is not inevitable While large language models present real risks to society, experts say they can be tested and largely controlled using well-worn cybersecurity and policy choices. ( Cyberscoop ) ‘Context Bombs’ Cut AI Attack Success by Misleading Agents With Fake Targets Deceptive prompts lure AI agents into decoys and dead ends, cutting attack success by up to 91% in tests and raising the cost of a successful attack 23-fold.( SecurityWeek ) Can’t get enough Talos? Compromised eMudhra intermediate certificates Cisco Talos is aware of eight intermediate certificates belonging to the intermediate certificate authority, eMudhra. Parasitizing trust: How legitimate infrastructure becomes a delivery pipeline for attackers Adversaries are turning the tools businesses trust into delivery mechanisms for malicious activity. Cisco Talos observed abuse of more than 25 legitimate platforms over the past year, exploiting the built-in trust of collaboration, file-sharing, payment and other services to reach their targets. There's only so much code: the rise in vulnerability numbers The September Microsoft Patch Tuesday release included 975 vulnerability advisories. This month, 1,415 vulnerabilities were just dropped. Compared to a pre-June average of 100 a month, that increase is staggering. Where did they come from? And what does the future look like? Note: Ivanti’s Integrity Checker Tool may not detect evidence of exploitation of CVE-2026-104935 because threat actor commands execute in memory. CISA is aware of cyber threat actors exploiting this zero-day authentication bypass vulnerability, which allows remote, unauthenticated execution of arbitrary commands, to conduct credential theft and data exfiltration. CISA added CVE-2026-104935 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog on Oct. 13, 2026. CISA urges organizations with affected Ivanti Connect Secure appliances and deployments to immediately update to the latest version, as outlined in Ivanti’s Security Advisory Ivanti Connect Secure (CVE-2026-104935) . Organizations should also review the Ivanti Connect Secure 25.x Upgrade and Migration Compatibility Guide for detailed patching guidance for hardware and virtual appliance deployments. Ivanti Connect Secure version 22.8 reaches end of life on Jan. 31, 2027. Organizations seeking to determine whether they were compromised will need to conduct network and memory forensics to identify evidence of exploitation. Note: Ivanti’s Integrity Checker Tool may not detect evidence of exploitation of CVE-2026-104935 because threat actor commands execute in memory. If your organization suspects a compromise, CISA recommends implementing the following actions from Ivanti Connect Secure Recovery Procedures : Create a backup of the appliance configuration. Review Ivanti’s How to Backup & Restore the Binary Configuration Using Archiving Server for more information. Conduct a factory reset and upgrade the appliance to the latest version. For cloud and virtual systems, rebuild the virtual instance and upgrade to the latest version. Restore the appliance configuration from the backup created in step 1. Reset passwords for all accounts, including domain, administrator, and local accounts. Revoke and reissue stored certificates; reset stored API keys and license server credentials. CISA urges organizations to review the Ivanti security advisory and guide noted above and apply necessary updates. CISA also recommends reviewing the Volexity blog, A Series of Unauthenticated Events: Chained Exploitation of Ivanti Connect Secure Zero-Days . objectives.falsification_criterion: If MDM / patch-management shows 100% deployment of the CVE-2026-104935 fix across exposed hosts, the hypothesis is disproven by remediation.
objectives.suggested_query: patch_state | where kb in (fixes_for('CVE-2026-104935')) | summarize coverage = avg(installed) by host_role

objectives.title: Post-exploit web-shell sweep
objectives.falsification_criterion: If a sweep of webroots and IIS/Apache process trees finds no anomalous children (cmd, powershell, /bin/sh) on Ivanti Connect Secure hosts, post-exploit foothold is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: process | where parent in ('w3wp.exe','httpd','nginx','java') and child in ('cmd.exe','powershell.exe','/bin/sh','/bin/bash')

objectives.title: Honeypot / canary check
objectives.falsification_criterion: If exposed canary instances of the same product show no probing or exploitation telemetry, opportunistic mass-exploitation against the org is unlikely.
objectives.suggested_query: canary_events | where product == '<product>' | where event_type in ('probe','exploit') | summarize by src_ip

hypotheses.title: Outbound C2 beaconing to reported infrastructure
hypotheses.statement: Hosts in the estate are beaconing to the command-and-control infrastructure reported in this article (domains, IPs, TLS fingerprints, or RMM tooling).
hypotheses.rationale: Archetype 'c2_beacon' selected based on CVEs cited: CVE-2026-104935; vectors: exploit, vpn-edge, credential-theft; impact: fraud; products: Ivanti Connect Secure.

objectives.title: DNS resolution sweep for published C2 domains
objectives.falsification_criterion: If recursive DNS logs show zero resolutions for the IOC domains in the last 90 days, active beaconing is disproven.
objectives.suggested_query: dns | where query in ('the published C2 domains') | summarize count() by client_ip

objectives.title: Egress connections to published C2 IPs
objectives.falsification_criterion: If proxy / firewall egress logs show no connections to the IOC IPs or matching ASNs, network-level C2 is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: egress | where dst_ip in ('25.1.1.1','25.1.2.2') | summarize bytes_out = sum(bytes_sent) by src_ip

objectives.title: Beacon periodicity / jitter analysis
objectives.falsification_criterion: If beacon-style periodic outbound connections (low jitter, small payloads) to uncategorised destinations are absent, covert C2 is unlikely.
objectives.suggested_query: conn | summarize stddev_interval = stdev(diff(ts)), count() by src_ip, dst_host | where count() > 50 and stddev_interval < 5s

objectives.title: TLS / JA3 fingerprint pivot
objectives.falsification_criterion: If JA3/JA3S fingerprints associated with the reported family are absent in TLS telemetry, encrypted C2 attribution is weakened.
objectives.suggested_query: tls | where ja3 in (ti_lookup('family','ja3')) | summarize by src_ip, sni

objectives.falsification_criterion: If unmanaged AnyDesk / TeamViewer / ScreenConnect / Atera installs are absent, RMM-based C2 is disproven.
objectives.suggested_query: process | where name in ('anydesk.exe','teamviewer.exe','screenconnect.exe','atera*.exe') and signer != 'corp_managed'

hypotheses.title: Identity compromise of privileged users
hypotheses.statement: Privileged identities have been compromised through phishing, MFA fatigue, help-desk social engineering, or OAuth illicit-consent grants.
hypotheses.rationale: Archetype 'identity_compromise' selected based on CVEs cited: CVE-2026-104935; vectors: exploit, vpn-edge, credential-theft; impact: fraud; products: Ivanti Connect Secure.

objectives.title: Impossible-travel / atypical sign-ins
objectives.falsification_criterion: If Entra ID / Okta risky-sign-in detections show no impossible-travel hits on privileged identities, account compromise is unsupported.

objectives.title: MFA-fatigue / push-bombing

Minimize network exposure for all control system devices and/or systems, ensuring they are not accessible from the internet. hypotheses.title: Initial access via CVE-2023-52927 affecting Linux kernel
hypotheses.statement: A threat actor has attempted to obtain initial access to our environment by exploiting CVE-2023-52927 in Linux kernel within the last 30 days.
hypotheses.rationale: Archetype 'initial_access_cve' selected based on CVEs cited: CVE-2023-52927, CVE-2023-53292, CVE-2023-54271; vectors: exploit, vpn-edge; products: Linux kernel.

objectives.title: Inventory exposure to Linux kernel
objectives.falsification_criterion: If zero internet-facing assets run a vulnerable build of Linux kernel, the external-exploitation hypothesis is disproven for CVE-2023-52927.
objectives.suggested_query: asset_inventory | where product == 'Linux kernel' and exposure == 'internet' and version in (vulnerable_versions)

objectives.title: Hunt for exploit attempts at the edge
objectives.falsification_criterion: If WAF / firewall / IDS show no exploit-signature hits for CVE-2023-52927 in the last 30 days, in-the-wild exploitation against us is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: edge_logs | where signature contains 'CVE' or uri matches /exploit-pattern-for-CVE-2023-52927/ | summarize count() by src_ip, dst_host

objectives.title: Patch-status correlation
objectives.falsification_criterion: If MDM / patch-management shows 100% deployment of the CVE-2023-52927 fix across exposed hosts, the hypothesis is disproven by remediation.
objectives.suggested_query: patch_state | where kb in (fixes_for('CVE-2023-52927')) | summarize coverage = avg(installed) by host_role

objectives.title: Post-exploit web-shell sweep
objectives.falsification_criterion: If a sweep of webroots and IIS/Apache process trees finds no anomalous children (cmd, powershell, /bin/sh) on Linux kernel hosts, post-exploit foothold is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: process | where parent in ('w3wp.exe','httpd','nginx','java') and child in ('cmd.exe','powershell.exe','/bin/sh','/bin/bash')

objectives.title: Honeypot / canary check
objectives.falsification_criterion: If exposed canary instances of the same product show no probing or exploitation telemetry, opportunistic mass-exploitation against the org is unlikely.
objectives.suggested_query: canary_events | where product == '<product>' | where event_type in ('probe','exploit') | summarize by src_ip

hypotheses.title: Outbound C2 beaconing to reported infrastructure
hypotheses.statement: Hosts in the estate are beaconing to the command-and-control infrastructure reported in this article (domains, IPs, TLS fingerprints, or RMM tooling).
hypotheses.rationale: Archetype 'c2_beacon' selected based on CVEs cited: CVE-2023-52927, CVE-2023-53292, CVE-2023-54271; vectors: exploit, vpn-edge; products: Linux kernel.

objectives.title: DNS resolution sweep for published C2 domains
objectives.falsification_criterion: If recursive DNS logs show zero resolutions for the IOC domains in the last 90 days, active beaconing is disproven.
objectives.suggested_query: dns | where query in ('www.siemens.com') | summarize count() by client_ip

objectives.title: Egress connections to published C2 IPs
objectives.falsification_criterion: If proxy / firewall egress logs show no connections to the IOC IPs or matching ASNs, network-level C2 is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: egress | where dst_ip in ('the published C2 IPs') | summarize bytes_out = sum(bytes_sent) by src_ip

objectives.title: Beacon periodicity / jitter analysis
objectives.falsification_criterion: If beacon-style periodic outbound connections (low jitter, small payloads) to uncategorised destinations are absent, covert C2 is unlikely.
objectives.suggested_query: conn | summarize stddev_interval = stdev(diff(ts)), count() by src_ip, dst_host | where count() > 50 and stddev_interval < 5s

objectives.title: TLS / JA3 fingerprint pivot
objectives.falsification_criterion: If JA3/JA3S fingerprints associated with the reported family are absent in TLS telemetry, encrypted C2 attribution is weakened.
objectives.suggested_query: tls | where ja3 in (ti_lookup('family','ja3')) | summarize by src_ip, sni

objectives.title: Remote-monitoring tooling abuse check
objectives.falsification_criterion: If unmanaged AnyDesk / TeamViewer / ScreenConnect / Atera installs are absent, RMM-based C2 is disproven.
objectives.suggested_query: process | where name in ('anydesk.exe','teamviewer.exe','screenconnect.exe','atera*.exe') and signer != 'corp_managed'

hypotheses.title: Identity compromise of privileged users
hypotheses.statement: Privileged identities have been compromised through phishing, MFA fatigue, help-desk social engineering, or OAuth illicit-consent grants.
hypotheses.rationale: Archetype 'identity_compromise' selected based on CVEs cited: CVE-2023-52927, CVE-2023-53292, CVE-2023-54271; vectors: exploit, vpn-edge; products: Linux kernel.

objectives.title: Impossible-travel / atypical sign-ins
objectives.falsification_criterion: If Entra ID / Okta risky-sign-in detections show no impossible-travel hits on privileged identities, account compromise is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: signin | where risk_level in ('high','medium') and user in (privileged_users) | summarize by country, ip

objectives.title: MFA-fatigue / push-bombing
objectives.falsification_criterion: If MFA telemetry shows no bursts of denied pushes followed by a successful one for the same user, MFA-fatigue compromise is disproven.
objectives.suggested_query: mfa | summarize denies = countif(result=='deny'), accepts = countif(result=='accept') by user, bin(ts,1h) | where denies > 5 and accepts > 0

objectives.title: Help-desk social-engineering pivot
objectives.falsification_criterion: If ticketing / call-recording shows no recent password-reset or MFA-reset requests for privileged users without proper verification, help-desk vector is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: tickets | where action in ('password_reset','mfa_reset') and target in (privileged_users) | join (verifications) on ticket_id

objectives.title: OAuth illicit-consent grants
objectives.falsification_criterion: If Entra/Workspace audit logs show no recently consented third-party apps with high-impact scopes, OAuth abuse is disproven.
objectives.suggested_query: audit | where action == 'Consent to application' and scopes contains 'Mail.Read' or 'files.read.all'

article.title: Hitachi Energy MicroSCADA X SYS600 Product
article.summary: View CSAF Summary Hitachi Energy is aware of multiple vulnerabilities that affect MicroSCADA X SYS600 product versions listed in this document. These vulnerabilities can be exploited to carry out various attacks on the product. Please refer to the Recommended Immediate Actions for information about the mitigation/remediation. The following versions of Hitachi Energy MicroSCADA X SYS600 Product are affected: MicroSCADA X SYS600 vers:MicroSCADA_X_SYS600/ CVSS Vendor Equipment v3 7.8 Hitachi Energy MicroSCADA X SYS600 2 Vulnerabilities Improper Neutralization of Formula Elements in a CSV File, Incorrect Implementation of Authentication Algorithm Background Critical Infrastructure Sectors: Energy Countries/Areas Deployed: Worldwide Company Headquarters Location: Switzerland Vulnerabilities Expand All + CVE-2026-9852 A CSV injection vulnerability exists in SYS600. Injected malicious formulas can add or modify data to the spreadsheet, insert links, exfiltrate data, and in some cases, depending on how the user has their environment configured, execute malicious code on the user’s machine. To exploit this issue attackers would need a way to create arbitrary log messages. This could be achieved through normal functionality via SCIL scripts, a log injection vulnerability, or via the SYS600 broker. This vulnerability affects all Windows users regardless of their privilege level who can run the Notify service and export the log. Read More 1 Affected Product MicroSCADA X SYS600 versions 1

Process control systems should not be used for Internet surfing, instant messaging, or receiving e-mails. Portable computers and removable storage media should be carefully scanned for viruses before they are connected to a control system. Proper password policies and processes should be followed. Additional information on Industrial Control Systems Cybersecurity Best Practices can be found in the Hitachi Energy’s “Industrial Control Systems Cybersecurity Best Practices” Cybersecurity Notification. objectives.title: Post-exploit web-shell sweep
objectives.falsification_criterion: If a sweep of webroots and IIS/Apache process trees finds no anomalous children (cmd, powershell, /bin/sh) on the affected product hosts, post-exploit foothold is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: process | where parent in ('w3wp.exe','httpd','nginx','java') and child in ('cmd.exe','powershell.exe','/bin/sh','/bin/bash')

objectives.title: Honeypot / canary check
objectives.falsification_criterion: If exposed canary instances of the same product show no probing or exploitation telemetry, opportunistic mass-exploitation against the org is unlikely.
objectives.suggested_query: canary_events | where product == '<product>' | where event_type in ('probe','exploit') | summarize by src_ip

hypotheses.title: Outbound C2 beaconing to reported infrastructure
hypotheses.statement: Hosts in the estate are beaconing to the command-and-control infrastructure reported in this article (domains, IPs, TLS fingerprints, or RMM tooling).

objectives.title: DNS resolution sweep for published C2 domains
objectives.falsification_criterion: If recursive DNS logs show zero resolutions for the IOC domains in the last 90 days, active beaconing is disproven.
objectives.suggested_query: dns | where query in ('www.cisa.gov') | summarize count() by client_ip

objectives.title: Egress connections to published C2 IPs
objectives.falsification_criterion: If proxy / firewall egress logs show no connections to the IOC IPs or matching ASNs, network-level C2 is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: egress | where dst_ip in ('the published C2 IPs') | summarize bytes_out = sum(bytes_sent) by src_ip

objectives.title: Beacon periodicity / jitter analysis
objectives.falsification_criterion: If beacon-style periodic outbound connections (low jitter, small payloads) to uncategorised destinations are absent, covert C2 is unlikely.

article.raw_text: Siemens RUGGEDCOM APE1808 Devices View CSAF Summary Nozomi Networks has published information on vulnerabilities in Nozomi Guardian/CMC. This advisory lists the related Siemens Industrial products affected by these vulnerabilities. Siemens recommends to contact customer support to receive patch and update information. The following versions of Siemens RUGGEDCOM APE1808 Devices are affected: RUGGEDCOM APE1808 vers:all/* (CVE-2026-33387, CVE-2026-33388, CVE-2026-33389, CVE-2026-33391, CVE-2026-33920) CVSS Vendor Equipment v3 7.5 Siemens RUGGEDCOM APE1808 4 Vulnerabilities Improper Neutralization of Special Elements Used in a Template Engine, Incorrect Authorization, Lack of Administrator Control over Security, Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) Background Critical Infrastructure Sectors: Critical Manufacturing, Transportation Systems, Energy, Healthcare and Public Health, Financial Services, Government Services and Facilities Countries/Areas Deployed: Worldwide Company Headquarters Location: Germany Vulnerabilities Expand All + CVE-2026-33387 A template injection vulnerability was discovered in the Dashboards functionality due to improper validation of an input parameter. An authenticated user with the required privileges can define a dashboard containing a malicious payload, or a victim can be socially engineered into importing a malicious dashboard. When the victim views or imports the dashboard, the payload executes in their browser context, allowing the attacker to modify application data or disrupt application availability. Read More 1 Affected Product RUGGEDCOM APE1808 with Nozomi Guardian/CMC Product Status: known_affected Remediations Vendor fix Contact customer support to receive patch and update information Additional Metrics Relevant CWE: CWE-1336 Improper Neutralization of Special Elements Used in a Template Engine CVSS Version Base Score Base Severity Vector String 3.1 4.6 MEDIUM CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:R/S:U/C:N/I:L/A:L View CVE Details CVE-2026-33388 An access control vulnerability was discovered in the Credentials Manager functionality due to insufficient validation of user privileges. A remote authenticated user with limited privileges can view a limited subset of the available entries in the Credentials Manager. The actual credential values are not directly visible, but the user can delete entries or edit their properties. An attacker who deletes or edits an entry can disrupt authentication for dependent devices, and one who manipulates an entry's configuration may be able to indirectly obtain the credentials. Read More 2 Affected Products RUGGEDCOM APE1808 with Nozomi Guardian/CMC Product Status: known_affected Remediations Vendor fix Contact customer support to receive patch and update information RUGGEDCOM APE1808 with Nozomi Guardian/CMC Product Status: known_affected Remediations Vendor fix Contact customer support to receive patch and update information Additional Metrics Relevant CWE: CWE-863 Incorrect Authorization CVSS Version Base Score Base Severity Vector String 3.1 7.4 HIGH CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:C/C:L/I:L/A:L View CVE Details CVE-2026-33389 An improper certificate/host key validation vulnerability was discovered in the Smart Polling functionality, which established encrypted connections to target devices without validating the remote host's identity, and no option was provided to enable it. A man-in-the-middle attacker positioned between a sensor and a polled device can, during a polling session, impersonate the device and intercept the communication, including the credentials used to access it. The captured credentials can then be replayed to authenticate against the device itself or against other devices sharing the same credentials, allowing the attacker to access and tamper with the device's data and to disrupt its operations. Read More 3 Affected Products RUGGEDCOM APE1808 with Nozomi Guardian/CMC Product Status: known_affected Remediations Vendor fix Contact customer support to receive patch and update information RUGGEDCOM APE1808 with Nozomi Guardian/CMC Product Status: known_affected Remediations Vendor fix Contact customer support to receive patch and update information RUGGEDCOM APE1808 with Nozomi Guardian/CMC Product Status: known_affected Remediations Vendor fix Contact customer support to receive patch and update information Additional Metrics Relevant CWE: CWE-671 Lack of Administrator Control over Security CVSS Version Base Score Base Severity Vector String 3.1 7.5 HIGH CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:N/UI:R/S:C/C:H/I:L/A:L View CVE Details CVE-2026-33391 An access control vulnerability was discovered in the Smart Polling configuration functionality due to insufficient validation of user privileges. An authenticated user with limited privileges can remotely bypass the intended access control of the web management interface and modify the Smart Polling discovery configuration. This allows the attacker to disrupt the visibility of assets in the monitored network. Read More 4 Affected Products RUGGEDCOM APE1808 with Nozomi Guardian/CMC Product Status: known_affected Remediations Vendor fix Contact customer support to receive patch and update information RUGGEDCOM APE1808 with Nozomi Guardian/CMC Product Status: known_affected Remediations Vendor fix Contact customer support to receive patch and update information RUGGEDCOM APE1808 with Nozomi Guardian/CMC Product Status: known_affected Remediations Vendor fix Contact customer support to receive patch and update information RUGGEDCOM APE1808 with Nozomi Guardian/CMC Product Status: known_affected Remediations Vendor fix Contact customer support to receive patch and update information Additional Metrics Relevant CWE: CWE-863 Incorrect Authorization CVSS Version Base Score Base Severity Vector String 3.1 5.4 MEDIUM CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:L/A:L View CVE Details CVE-2026-33920 A cross-site request forgery vulnerability was discovered in the login functionality (both standard and SAML) due to missing validation of the anti-CSRF token. An attacker with a valid account can trick a victim into unknowingly authenticating with the attacker's credentials. Any operation performed by the victim in this state is attributed to the attacker's account, compromising the integrity of the audit trail. Read More 5 Affected Products RUGGEDCOM APE1808 with Nozomi Guardian/CMC Product Status: known_affected Remediations Vendor fix Contact customer support to receive patch and update information RUGGEDCOM APE1808 with Nozomi Guardian/CMC Product Status: known_affected Remediations Vendor fix Contact customer support to receive patch and update information RUGGEDCOM APE1808 with Nozomi Guardian/CMC Product Status: known_affected Remediations Vendor fix Contact customer support to receive patch and update information RUGGEDCOM APE1808 with Nozomi Guardian/CMC Product Status: known_affected Remediations Vendor fix Contact customer support to receive patch and update information RUGGEDCOM APE1808 with Nozomi Guardian/CMC Product Status: known_affected Remediations Vendor fix Contact customer support to receive patch and update information Additional Metrics Relevant CWE: CWE-352 Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) CVSS Version Base Score Base Severity Vector String 3.1 3.5 LOW CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:R/S:U/C:N/I:L/A:N View CVE Details Acknowledgments Siemens ProductCERT reported these vulnerabilities to CISA. General Recommendations As a general security measure, Siemens strongly recommends to protect network access to devices with appropriate mechanisms. In order to operate the devices in a protected IT environment, Siemens recommends to configure the environment according to Siemens' operational guidelines for Industrial Security (Download: https://www.siemens.com/cert/operational-guidelines-industrial-security), and to follow the recommendations in the product manuals. Additional information on Industrial Security by Siemens can be found at: https://www.siemens.com/industrialsecurity Additional Resources For further inquiries on security vulnerabilities in Siemens products and solutions, please contact the Siemens ProductCERT: https://www.siemens.com/cert/advisories Terms of Use The use of Siemens Security Advisories is subject to the terms and conditions listed on: https://www.siemens.com/productcert/terms-of-use. Minimize network exposure for all control system devices and/or systems, ensuring they are not accessible from the internet . Locate control system networks and remote devices behind firewalls and isolating them from business networks. When remote access is required, use more secure methods, such as Virtual Private Networks (VPNs), recognizing VPNs may have vulnerabilities and should be updated to the most current version available. Also recognize VPN is only as secure as the connected devices. CISA reminds organizations to perform proper impact analysis and risk assessment prior to deploying defensive measures. CISA also provides a section for control systems security recommended practices on the ICS webpage on cisa.gov/ics . Several CISA products detailing cyber defense best practices are available for reading and download, including Improving Industrial Control Systems Cybersecurity with Defense-in-Depth Strategies . CISA encourages organizations to implement recommended cybersecurity strategies for proactive defense of ICS assets . Additional mitigation guidance and recommended practices are publicly available on the ICS webpage at cisa.gov/ics in the technical information paper, ICS-TIP-12-146-01B--Targeted Cyber Intrusion Detection and Mitigation Strategies . Organizations observing suspected malicious activity should follow established internal procedures and report findings to CISA for tracking and correlation against other incidents. article.title: CISA Adds Four Known Exploited Vulnerabilities to Catalog
article.summary: CISA has added four new vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog , based on evidence of active exploitation. CVE-2026-0322 Palo Alto Networks PAN-OS Code Injection Vulnerability CVE-2026-76519 Cisco Secure Email Gateway Relative Path Traversal Vulnerability CVE-2026-105133 Ahsay AhsayCBS Improper Authentication Vulnerability CVE-2026-105134 Ahsay AhsayCBS Command Injection Vulnerability These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise. Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied. While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities . CISA will continue

article.title: Panchan's Mining Island [Guest Diary], (Wed, Oct 14th)
article.summary: [This is a Guest Diary by Zachary Norwood, an ISC intern as part of the SANS.edu BACS program]
article.raw_text: Panchan's Mining Island [Guest Diary], (Wed, Oct 14th) [This is a Guest Diary by Zachary Norwood, an ISC intern as part of the SANS.edu BACS program] [This is a Guest Diary by Zachary Norwood, an ISC intern as part of the SANS.edu BACS program] Crypto mining malware has been active and spreading across the internet for quite some time now. Moreover, the DShield honeypot picked up a worm that self-propagates through a plethora of means. One of them is stealing SSH keys after it gains access to a system. Furthermore, it also leverages a rootkit to maintain access to infected systems. One would hope that threat actors would have moved on past this worm by now. However, due to its rudimentary design and its effectiveness, they have had no reason to move on. A malicious binary was uploaded and executed on the DShield honeypot, and that is where a copy of the Panchan worm was obtained. It is written with Golang, and it is a peer-to-peer botnet. Moreover, this worm was first identified in 2022. Many vendors recognize this worm now as seen below. VirusTotal Clamscan Therefore, a system with security controls such as egress filtering, ingress filtering, access control lists, continuous monitoring, and passwordless authentication will prevent this worm from taking root. However, many systems are insecure and unpatched. This is why this worm is still propagating across the internet. The strings captured from the binary below show how simple it is to find its command-and-control channel and the functions that it consists of. Furthermore, leveraging something as simple as syslog to pull logs and using commands such as grep to find privilege escalation activities, software installation, software removal, and access to ports such as SSH will allow an analyst to identify this activity. However, this does not scale well. Therefore, leveraging a SIEM to gather and parse this data is a much more effective solution. Next, all traffic entering and exiting from both the trusted and untrusted networks needs to pass through at least one firewall. Preferably, also having an intrusion detection or prevention system right after the public facing firewall in the trusted zone. Command and Control Channel Panchan Functions These captures clearly show the source files that the Panchan worm consists of. To dig deeper into what this binary can do, a network simulator was used. Moreover, the specific network simulator that was used was FakeNet-NG with Wireshark to intercept the network traffic. These tools were used to identify what URL it was reaching out to once it was installed on a system. FakeNet-NG is a tool developed by the Mandiant FLARE team for dynamic network analysis. This tool simulates legitimate network traffic, allowing an analyst to identify how the malware interacts with the network and if it is communicating with an external server. This specific strain of this worm was using a discord channel as a command-and-control server. This was identified by capturing and dissecting the network traffic that was generated by the worm interacting with the FakeNet-NG network. FAKENET-NG Wireshark Capture Panchan, the peer-to-peer crypto mining worm, is a threat to any organization who has internet facing servers. This worm is mainly a threat to insecure systems, and opening SSH to a public network needs to be done in a secure way. Fail2Ban is a service that scans log files for repeated failed login attempts. This service then blocks that IP address by updating the system’s firewall rule. Fail2Ban is another control that should be put in place with a public facing SSH port. Services like SSH should have multi-factor authentication, and an access control list. The access control list should include specific IP addresses or a jump box. Disabling root login with SSH is another essential security control that needs to be implemented. With SSH, public and private key pairs are another option for authentication. This will then create the capability to disable password authentication for the SSH service preventing brute force attacks. However, these key pairs are often created and forgotten about. This is a security concern, and SSH private keys are something that this worm is designed to steal. Once it has stolen a private key, it attempts to pivot to hosts in the running user’s SSH known_hosts file. A simple mitigation to protect the data within the known_hosts file is to use the HashKnownHosts option within a systems SSH configuration. Furthermore, it is best to mitigate long lived credentials and SSH key stealing by leveraging tools likeHashiCorp Vault to sign SSH certificates with short expirations. This ensures that reusing a key becomes highly impractical or even impossible. The user will authenticate to Vault with their credentials then they send their SSH public key to Vault for signing, and finally Vault then signs the SSH key. Then it returns the SSH certificate to the user. This certificate can be used to log in to any host configured to trust the Vault CA. Leveraging such infrastructure will also allow an organization to disable password authentication entirely for services like SSH. Furthermore, leveraging something as simple as syslog to pull logs and using commands such as grep to find privilege escalation activities, software installation, software removal, and access to ports such as SSH will allow an analyst to identify this activity. However, this does not scale well. Therefore, leveraging a SIEM to gather and parse this data is a much more effective solution. Next, all traffic entering and exiting from both the trusted and untrusted networks needs to pass through at least one firewall. Preferably, also having an intrusion detection or prevention system right after the public facing firewall in the trusted zone. Typical indicators of compromise for this worm include multiple failed authentication attempts via SSH, unusual resource usage on infected systems, and processes that cannot be killed by any means. This worm also creates hidden directories in the running users home directory or folders like /tmp. Often, these directories have names that are strings that have high amounts of entropy. For this strain of this worm, servers reaching out to services like Discord on a regular basis is another indicator of compromise that an analyst can look for. In conclusion, denying by default and allowing by exception is a vital strategy for systems facing untrusted networks. These same techniques that were discussed above can be used to protect critical public facing infrastructure from threat actors. objectives.title: Inventory exposure to the affected product

article.raw_text: Ivanti Connect Secure zero-day exploited in the wild (CVE-2026-104935) Overview On October 13, 2026, Ivanti published a security advisory for CVE-2026-104935 , a high-severity authentication bypass by spoofing ( CWE-290 ) affecting Ivanti Connect Secure (ICS). The vulnerability has a CVSSv3.0 score of 8.6 and allows a remote, unauthenticated attacker to execute arbitrary commands. Ivanti reports that exploitation in the wild has already occurred prior to disclosure, affecting a limited number of customers. This indicates that exploitation has been occurring as a zero-day vulnerability. The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) confirms exploitation in the wild, and added CVE-2026-104935 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog on the same day as the vendor's public disclosure. The digital forensics firm Volexity has published a detailed blog post describing the threat actor activity, which was detected in early October 2026. Volexity notes that in addition to leveraging CVE-2026-104935 as a zero-day, the threat actor also leveraged an as-yet unpatched privilege escalation vulnerability which Ivanti are planning to patch at a later date. According to the vendor, a portion of the vulnerability was initially discovered through its product security program and patched in the July 2026 release of 25.1.3.0 . Exploitation occurred while Ivanti was working to backport the fix to the remaining supported versions. Ivanti Connect Secure is a popular enterprise VPN solution and naturally sits on the edge of a corporate environment. The product has a history of being targeted by attackers, with zero-day exploitation of other vulnerabilities occurring back in both 2024 and 2025 . Given the confirmed exploitation, the ability to execute commands without authentication, along with the history of the product, Rapid7 recommends that organizations running affected versions apply the appropriate update on an emergency basis outside of normal patching cycles. Mitigation guidance Vendor-supplied updates are available to remediate CVE-2026-104935. Ivanti lists the following affected and resolved versions: Ivanti Connect Secure affected versions Resolved versions 25.1.1.1 and prior in the applicable code line 25.1.1.2 25.1.2.2 and prior in the applicable code line 25.1.3.0 , 25.1.3.1 22.8R2.4 and prior in the applicable code line 22.8R2.5 Note that the vendor advisory confirms that versions 22.7.x and below are unaffected. At the time of the advisory, Ivanti states that reliable indicators of compromise are not available, however Volexity have published several here . Rapid7 strongly recommends looking for signs of compromise even after the patch has been applied. Customers who suspect exploitation should follow the vendor's recovery steps . For the latest mitigation guidance, please refer to the vendor's security advisory . Rapid7 customers Exposure Command, Vulnerability Management, and Nexpose Exposure Command, Vulnerability Management, and Nexpose customers can assess exposure to CVE-2026-104935 with a vulnerability check expected to be available in the October 14 content release. Updates October 13, 2026 : Initial publication.

When remote access is required, use more secure methods, such as virtual private networks (VPNs), recognizing VPNs may have vulnerabilities and should be updated to the most recent version available. hypotheses.title: Initial access via CVE-2026-80466 affecting the affected product/service
hypotheses.statement: A threat actor has attempted to obtain initial access to our environment by exploiting CVE-2026-80466 in the affected product/service within the last 30 days.
hypotheses.rationale: Archetype 'initial_access_cve' selected based on CVEs cited: CVE-2026-80466, CVE-2026-88850; vectors: exploit, vpn-edge.

objectives.title: Inventory exposure to the affected product
objectives.falsification_criterion: If zero internet-facing assets run a vulnerable build of the affected product, the external-exploitation hypothesis is disproven for CVE-2026-80466.
objectives.suggested_query: asset_inventory | where product == 'the affected product' and exposure == 'internet' and version in (vulnerable_versions)

objectives.title: Hunt for exploit attempts at the edge
objectives.falsification_criterion: If WAF / firewall / IDS show no exploit-signature hits for CVE-2026-80466 in the last 30 days, in-the-wild exploitation against us is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: edge_logs | where signature contains 'CVE' or uri matches /exploit-pattern-for-CVE-2026-80466/ | summarize count() by src_ip, dst_host

objectives.title: Patch-status correlation
objectives.falsification_criterion: If MDM / patch-management shows 100% deployment of the CVE-2026-80466 fix across exposed hosts, the hypothesis is disproven by remediation.
objectives.suggested_query: patch_state | where kb in (fixes_for('CVE-2026-80466')) | summarize coverage = avg(installed) by host_role

objectives.title: Post-exploit web-shell sweep
objectives.falsification_criterion: If a sweep of webroots and IIS/Apache process trees finds no anomalous children (cmd, powershell, /bin/sh) on the affected product hosts, post-exploit foothold is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: process | where parent in ('w3wp.exe','httpd','nginx','java') and child in ('cmd.exe','powershell.exe','/bin/sh','/bin/bash')

objectives.title: Honeypot / canary check
objectives.falsification_criterion: If exposed canary instances of the same product show no probing or exploitation telemetry, opportunistic mass-exploitation against the org is unlikely.
objectives.suggested_query: canary_events | where product == '<product>' | where event_type in ('probe','exploit') | summarize by src_ip

hypotheses.title: Outbound C2 beaconing to reported infrastructure
hypotheses.statement: Hosts in the estate are beaconing to the command-and-control infrastructure reported in this article (domains, IPs, TLS fingerprints, or RMM tooling).
hypotheses.rationale: Archetype 'c2_beacon' selected based on CVEs cited: CVE-2026-80466, CVE-2026-88850; vectors: exploit, vpn-edge.

objectives.title: DNS resolution sweep for published C2 domains
objectives.falsification_criterion: If recursive DNS logs show zero resolutions for the IOC domains in the last 90 days, active beaconing is disproven.
objectives.suggested_query: dns | where query in ('www.wago.com') | summarize count() by client_ip

objectives.title: Egress connections to published C2 IPs
objectives.falsification_criterion: If proxy / firewall egress logs show no connections to the IOC IPs or matching ASNs, network-level C2 is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: egress | where dst_ip in ('the published C2 IPs') | summarize bytes_out = sum(bytes_sent) by src_ip

objectives.title: Beacon periodicity / jitter analysis
objectives.falsification_criterion: If beacon-style periodic outbound connections (low jitter, small payloads) to uncategorised destinations are absent, covert C2 is unlikely.
objectives.suggested_query: conn | summarize stddev_interval = stdev(diff(ts)), count() by src_ip, dst_host | where count() > 50 and stddev_interval < 5s

objectives.title: TLS / JA3 fingerprint pivot
objectives.falsification_criterion: If JA3/JA3S fingerprints associated with the reported family are absent in TLS telemetry, encrypted C2 attribution is weakened.
objectives.suggested_query: tls | where ja3 in (ti_lookup('family','ja3')) | summarize by src_ip, sni

objectives.title: Remote-monitoring tooling abuse check
objectives.falsification_criterion: If unmanaged AnyDesk / TeamViewer / ScreenConnect / Atera installs are absent, RMM-based C2 is disproven.
objectives.suggested_query: process | where name in ('anydesk.exe','teamviewer.exe','screenconnect.exe','atera*.exe') and signer != 'corp_managed'

hypotheses.title: Identity compromise of privileged users
hypotheses.statement: Privileged identities have been compromised through phishing, MFA fatigue, help-desk social engineering, or OAuth illicit-consent grants.
hypotheses.rationale: Archetype 'identity_compromise' selected based on CVEs cited: CVE-2026-80466, CVE-2026-88850; vectors: exploit, vpn-edge.

objectives.title: Impossible-travel / atypical sign-ins
objectives.falsification_criterion: If Entra ID / Okta risky-sign-in detections show no impossible-travel hits on privileged identities, account compromise is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: signin | where risk_level in ('high','medium') and user in (privileged_users) | summarize by country, ip

objectives.title: MFA-fatigue / push-bombing
objectives.falsification_criterion: If MFA telemetry shows no bursts of denied pushes followed by a successful one for the same user, MFA-fatigue compromise is disproven.
objectives.suggested_query: mfa | summarize denies = countif(result=='deny'), accepts = countif(result=='accept') by user, bin(ts,1h) | where denies > 5 and accepts > 0

objectives.title: Help-desk social-engineering pivot
objectives.falsification_criterion: If ticketing / call-recording shows no recent password-reset or MFA-reset requests for privileged users without proper verification, help-desk vector is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: tickets | where action in ('password_reset','mfa_reset') and target in (privileged_users) | join (verifications) on ticket_id

objectives.title: OAuth illicit-consent grants
objectives.falsification_criterion: If Entra/Workspace audit logs show no recently consented third-party apps with high-impact scopes, OAuth abuse is disproven.
objectives.suggested_query: audit | where action == 'Consent to application' and scopes contains 'Mail.Read' or 'files.read.all'

article.title: CISA Adds Six Known Exploited Vulnerabilities to Catalog
article.summary: CISA has added six new vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog , based on evidence of active exploitation. article.raw_text: CISA Adds Six Known Exploited Vulnerabilities to Catalog CISA has added six new vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog , based on evidence of active exploitation. CVE-2026-96652 Plex Media Server Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) Vulnerability CVE-2026-96654 Plex Media Server Improper Neutralization of Encoded URI Schemes in a Web Page Vulnerability CVE-2026-96655 Plex Media Server Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) Vulnerability CVE-2026-96656 Plex Media Server External Control of File Name or Path Vulnerability CVE-2026-106931 EG Secure Solutions SiteGuard Server Edition OS Command Injection Vulnerability CVE-2026-110936 Siemens Software Center Uncontrolled Search Path Element Vulnerability These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise. Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied. While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities . CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria . Aware of an exploited vulnerability not currently listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form . Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.

hypotheses.rationale: Archetype 'c2_beacon' selected based on CVEs cited: CVE-2026-96652, CVE-2026-96654, CVE-2026-96655; vectors: exploit.

objectives.title: DNS resolution sweep for published C2 domains
objectives.falsification_criterion: If recursive DNS logs show zero resolutions for the IOC domains in the last 90 days, active beaconing is disproven.
objectives.suggested_query: dns | where query in ('the published C2 domains') | summarize count() by client_ip

objectives.title: Egress connections to published C2 IPs
objectives.falsification_criterion: If proxy / firewall egress logs show no connections to the IOC IPs or matching ASNs, network-level C2 is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: egress | where dst_ip in ('the published C2 IPs') | summarize bytes_out = sum(bytes_sent) by src_ip

objectives.title: Beacon periodicity / jitter analysis
objectives.falsification_criterion: If beacon-style periodic outbound connections (low jitter, small payloads) to uncategorised destinations are absent, covert C2 is unlikely.
objectives.suggested_query: conn | summarize stddev_interval = stdev(diff(ts)), count() by src_ip, dst_host | where count() > 50 and stddev_interval < 5s

objectives.title: TLS / JA3 fingerprint pivot
objectives.falsification_criterion: If JA3/JA3S fingerprints associated with the reported family are absent in TLS telemetry, encrypted C2 attribution is weakened.
objectives.suggested_query: tls | where ja3 in (ti_lookup('family','ja3')) | summarize by src_ip, sni

objectives.title: Remote-monitoring tooling abuse check
objectives.falsification_criterion: If unmanaged AnyDesk / TeamViewer / ScreenConnect / Atera installs are absent, RMM-based C2 is disproven.
objectives.suggested_query: process | where name in ('anydesk.exe','teamviewer.exe','screenconnect.exe','atera*.exe') and signer != 'corp_managed'

hypotheses.title: Identity compromise of privileged users
hypotheses.statement: Privileged identities have been compromised through phishing, MFA fatigue, help-desk social engineering, or OAuth illicit-consent grants.
hypotheses.rationale: Archetype 'identity_compromise' selected based on CVEs cited: CVE-2026-96652, CVE-2026-96654, CVE-2026-96655; vectors: exploit.

objectives.title: Impossible-travel / atypical sign-ins
objectives.falsification_criterion: If Entra ID / Okta risky-sign-in detections show no impossible-travel hits on privileged identities, account compromise is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: signin | where risk_level in ('high','medium') and user in (privileged_users) | summarize by country, ip

objectives.title: MFA-fatigue / push-bombing
objectives.falsification_criterion: If MFA telemetry shows no bursts of denied pushes followed by a successful one for the same user, MFA-fatigue compromise is disproven.
objectives.suggested_query: mfa | summarize denies = countif(result=='deny'), accepts = countif(result=='accept') by user, bin(ts,1h) | where denies > 5 and accepts > 0

objectives.title: Help-desk social-engineering pivot
objectives.falsification_criterion: If ticketing / call-recording shows no recent password-reset or MFA-reset requests for privileged users without proper verification, help-desk vector is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: tickets | where action in ('password_reset','mfa_reset') and target in (privileged_users) | join (verifications) on ticket_id

objectives.title: OAuth illicit-consent grants
objectives.falsification_criterion: If Entra/Workspace audit logs show no recently consented third-party apps with high-impact scopes, OAuth abuse is disproven.
objectives.suggested_query: audit | where action == 'Consent to application' and scopes contains 'Mail.Read' or 'files.read.all'

hypotheses.title: Initial access via CVE-2025-61624 affecting Fortinet FortiOS
hypotheses.statement: A threat actor has attempted to obtain initial access to our environment by exploiting CVE-2025-61624 in Fortinet FortiOS within the last 30 days.
hypotheses.rationale: Archetype 'initial_access_cve' selected based on CVEs cited: CVE-2025-61624, CVE-2026-102764; vectors: exploit, vpn-edge; products: Fortinet FortiOS.

objectives.title: Inventory exposure to Fortinet FortiOS
objectives.falsification_criterion: If zero internet-facing assets run a vulnerable build of Fortinet FortiOS, the external-exploitation hypothesis is disproven for CVE-2025-61624.
objectives.suggested_query: asset_inventory | where product == 'Fortinet FortiOS' and exposure == 'internet' and version in (vulnerable_versions)

objectives.title: Hunt for exploit attempts at the edge
objectives.falsification_criterion: If WAF / firewall / IDS show no exploit-signature hits for CVE-2025-61624 in the last 30 days, in-the-wild exploitation against us is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: edge_logs | where signature contains 'CVE' or uri matches /exploit-pattern-for-CVE-2025-61624/ | summarize count() by src_ip, dst_host

objectives.title: Patch-status correlation
objectives.falsification_criterion: If MDM / patch-management shows 100% deployment of the CVE-2025-61624 fix across exposed hosts, the hypothesis is disproven by remediation.
objectives.suggested_query: patch_state | where kb in (fixes_for('CVE-2025-61624')) | summarize coverage = avg(installed) by host_role

objectives.title: Post-exploit web-shell sweep
objectives.falsification_criterion: If a sweep of webroots and IIS/Apache process trees finds no anomalous children (cmd, powershell, /bin/sh) on Fortinet FortiOS hosts, post-exploit foothold is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: process | where parent in ('w3wp.exe','httpd','nginx','java') and child in ('cmd.exe','powershell.exe','/bin/sh','/bin/bash')

objectives.title: Honeypot / canary check
objectives.falsification_criterion: If exposed canary instances of the same product show no probing or exploitation telemetry, opportunistic mass-exploitation against the org is unlikely.
objectives.suggested_query: canary_events | where product == '<product>' | where event_type in ('probe','exploit') | summarize by src_ip

article.title: Attackers Exploit AhsayCBS Flaws to Deploy XMRig Miners Disguised as Microsoft Edge
article.summary: Threat actors have been observed exploiting two recently disclosed flaws in the AhsayCBS backup utility to seize control of affected devices and deploy web shells and XMRig cryptocurrency miners. Details of the flaws are below - CVE-2026-105133 (CVSS v4 score: 5.5) - An improper authentication vulnerability in the checkSysPwd() function in the "com/ahsay/obs/api/ApiStructsAction.java"
